ings and all her treasured art

cause them to collapse.

PRAGUE, Sept. 2.-The Prague
press said today that Czechoslovak
state courts were sending to jail
citizens accused of having knowl-
edge of anti-government plots and
failing to inform the police.


There was no information on
how many such suspects had been
rounded up. The trials usually are
secret.


The press indicated, however,
that a number of these "non-in-
formers" had been jailed in con-
nection with the armed revolt plot
which the government announced
Tuesday that it had crushed. The
government said the plot was
foiled just as participants were
moving to seize strategic points in
this capital city.


The Communist party organ,
Rude Pravo, said that among per-
sons tried in connection with re-
cent plots against the regime were
people with no criminal aims, but
just ordinary persons who failed
to inform the authorities about
criminal actions of others OF which
they had knowledge"


Rude Pravda said some OF these
non-informers actually regarded
anti-state plotting as disgusting. "
but ran afoul of the law because
they failed to perform their patri-
otic duty" and report to the police.


Disclosing criminal activities is
not tale-bearing. but the patriotic
duty of every citizen" the paper
said. ~ :


Rude Pravda also lashed anew
at the Western powers and the
Vatican as alleged hackers of plots
against the Czech government.


Tn the international reaction
fighting against our country all
the enemy powers have linked to-
gether," said the Communist Or
gan. "They include the imperialist
powers, their espionage services,
the expelled Sudeten Germans who
want to return, treacherous Czech
exiles and the Vatican"

BELGRADE, Yugoslavia, Oct

street knew today that his coun-
try was near the climax of a
David -and- Goliath struggle with
Russia which the whole world
watched with mounting anxiety.


The press had informed him
about the struggle which preceded
Yugoslavia's election today to a
seat on the United Nations Sc
curity Council, a struggle in which
the United States backed Premier
Marshal Tito against bitter Rus
sian opposition.


The average citizen displayed
intense excitement over the fight
to beat out Czechoslovakia for
the Council seat.


Through the Communist news
paper Borba, he also knew that
Tito's government had accused
Russia of moving troops into
neighbor Cominform countries in
the mounting war of nerves.


People Rally Around Tito.


There has been increasing evi-
dence here that the more Russia
attacks Tito, both In the United
Nations and elsewhere, the more
his proud. ruggedly individualistic
people rally around him.


The Yugoslav press told the cit
.izenry about the U. N. struggle.
The Communist newspaper Borba
used the story under this head
line: Election of Yugoslavia to
Security Council would increase
moral authority of U. NJ"


The newspaper Politika used this
headline: by putting her candi-
dacy before the Security Council,
Yugoslavia has no other aims ex-
cept guarding independence and
establishing equal rights among
countries


Equal rights" is the key to
the Moscow-Belgrade fight. Tito
has refused to bend to Moscow's
will and wants to be treated as
an equal.


Warmongering Charged.


The Yugoslavs charged last
night that Russian troop move
ments in the Cominform coun-
tries were aimed at building up
"warmongering" pressure against
the Tito regime.


I'm Trieste, a refugee Ro-

built under Russian supervision
along the Yugoslav borders in
Bulgaria, Hungary and Albania,
the paper declared.


Gn Athens, well-informed


intelligence officers said pri-
vately that Russia has placed


five divisions along the Yugo-


slav borders in the last month.


CThese sources - American,


British and Greek-said Rus


sia apparently feared that Tito


was secretly backing plans for


a revolt in the isolated Soviet


satellite of Albania.)

France and the United States have been
exchanging gifts for long time One of
them was Lafayette, and another was
Pershing. The THANK You Train which
arrived. in Washington date Saturday night
is but an additional symbol Of the good
will and the mutually which bind the two
great republics.


Characteristically, both this train and
the Friendship Train which it acknowl
edges have been the result of independent
initiative. Six million French citizens sent
these cars to America to say "Merci'' to
all the contributors to the earlier enter
prise in aid of France. Each of the thou
sands of gifts to be distributed from the
Thank You Train represents an individual
choice, a personal gesture Of gratitude.
People, not simply organized governments,
are speaking to each other.


Such exchanges are possible only between
free communities. Totalitarian states have
no such funds of natural popular feeling
upon which to draw. Societies which are
regimented by dictators and patterned to
planned economies are robbed of their
humane endowments. After that pilfering
has been completed, they have nothing
left to give save slavish obedience to their
masters. Spontaneous expression perishes
in them Their arts become propaganda
for fixed idea, their sciences are stulti-
fed to single arbitrary dogma.


Providentially, France and the United
States still have their liberty. So the
Friendship Train and the Thank You Train
have been spiritual experiences. They
have drawn the two nations. the two peo-
Piles closer together. Indeed, they exem-
plify the mystic principle Of the Psalmist:
Behold, how good and how pleasant 1t Is
for brethren to dwell together in unity:"

|. The paper quoted well-informed
sources as reporting that members
of the Polish military mission here
acted as intermediate about two
weeks ago.


Social Democrat did not further

vague. The paper said the Rus
slams had offered to lift the block
ade of Berlin if the Western
powers would enter into negotia-

currency for Berlin.

Europe's air.

dollars as before currency devalu-

plane.

Association yesterday agreed to
cut rates for dollar-paying pas

East, Asia and Africa. Spokes-

per cent.

tinue. For passengers paying in
devalued currency, the fares across
the Atlantic will 60 up, to COM
pensate for the devaluation.


The new rates. effective October
/, will continue in force at least
until the IATA meets November
in Mexico City.

The two big unions-one anti

Thousands of pretty girls

Other thousands took their cars

Labor did not appear to be car
rying on any agitation now that
the strike was on. There were no
reports of clashes between strikers
and non strikers. No big demon
strations were scheduled. No un-

patrolling about or on bicycles.


Food Stores Stay Open.


Food stores everywhere were
open. Aperitif-loving Frenchmen
found all their cafes and bistros
doing business. Most banks and
the Paris stock exchange were at
work. A spokesman at the Postal
Ministry said the situation was
"about normal in the mail busi-
ness all over France.


Hotels reported their staffs at
normal strength. Telephone calls
were accepted to all parts of
France and abroad. There were no
newspapers in Paris, though, and
the state-owned radio was silent

during the day.


Frances equivalent of Macy'si

Printemps-said from 95 to 100

giers and New York were can
celled. But the airlines said planes

Madrid. Barcelona and London.

Copenhagen would run on time.

unanimous opposition to the
strike and determination not to
lose a days pay. Liberal and Con-
servative newspaper had de-
nounced the work stoppage,
expected to cost France 10,700.-
100000 francs (about $30. 900 .000).


French observers said today's
strike was a pale imitation Of
prewar general strikes. like those
in 1919 and 1886. <

NEW YORK, Oct. 21.-A Ne
vada divorce still separated
father and mother today, despite
their 5-year-old sons legal effort
to cancel it.


The law suit to set aside the
decree. filed through the mother
as guardian, was dismissed here
yesterday by State Supreme Court
Justice Samuel II. Hofstadter.


He said the mother could not do
in the child's name what she could
not legally do herself.


The boys suit contended the
Reno court lacked jurisdiction.


Mrs. Francis Farah won the di-
vorce at Reno in 1945 from Henry
Farah, New York lingerie manu-
facturer.


The new suit, brought in the
name of their child, Ronald Henry
Farah, said the father misrepre-
sented his wealth in agreeing to
pay $55 week for the boys sup
port. The child asked for $4,000
damages.


When the suit was filed, the
boys attorney, Bernard Kaufman,
said Mrs. Farah could not sue
because she was party to the
divorce. He said the case would
be appealed.

More than 100000 gallons of
untreated sewage is emptied into
the Potomac River each day by the
City of Alexandria.


This is about four times the
amount that Fairfax County con-
tributes to Potomac pollution. But
unlike Fairfax, Alexandria has
struck no legal snarls in adding to
its sewer lines.


The comparative ease with which
Alexandria has continued to add
to the amount of effluent it empties
into the Potomac while Fairfax
has run afoul of the State Water
Control Board is due in large
measure, city officials believe, to
the relatively small sewer extern
sions needed for new building in
a highly developed community like
Alexandria. In Fairfax, however,
new developments that require
sewer service have had to install
miles of new sewer lines.


Plans for Disposal Plant.


Alexandria also has compelte
plans for sewage disposal plant,
while the proposal for such a plant
irAl Fairfax still is in the planning
stage. Fairfax recently was warned
by the State Water Control Board
against permitting further extern
sion of the Holmes Run trunk
sewer that serves the county's San
itary District No. l. County officials
were told at that time they should
have plans ready for a sewage
treatment plant before seeking per-
mission to extend sewers.


Alexandria's sewage disposal prof.
ect was outlined to the City Council
early in 1947 Since that time the
estimated cost of the project has
jumped from about $3,5OO,000 to
S4,0O0,000, figure city officials be-
lieve is too expensive.


The engineering firm of Greeley
g. Hansen prepared the sewer plan
for Alexandria. At present, the
city discharges sewage into Four
Mile Run at Commonwealth ave-
nue. and the north city limits; into
the Potomac River through many
outlets along the water front; into
Hunting Greek at Royal street; into
Hoof1S Run west of Duke street, and
into Hooffs Run near its junction
with Hunting Greek. The waters |
from all of the creeks and runs
mentioned flow into the Potomac.


Trunk Sewer Proposed.


The engineers proposed that sew
age from the Four Mile Run area,
from the Hooffs Run area, and from
other areas west of Hooffs Run be
emptied into a large intercepting
trunk sewer running along Com
avenue. Present sew
ers running easterly to the Potomac
would empty into a second large
trunk sewer extending
along the water front from Second !
street to Hunting Greek.


Under the proposal the disposal
plant should be located on the north
bank of Hunting Greek west of
Payne street. Both of the inter-
cepting trunk sewers would flow to
the disposal plant.


Annual cost of operation of the
necessary pumping stations and
treatment works would be from
81, 900 to $4,000, 1t was estimated.


Bond Issue Urged.


The engineers proposed that the
project be financed by sewer revenue
bonds, with users of the facility
paying a monthly fee for sewer
service. But a sewer service charge |
in Alexandria, where citizens have
city-f1nanced sewer service
would be unpopular.


Many residents already have
asked why Alexandra should 60
ahead with such an expensive prof.
ect while other communities con-
tinue to pollute the Potomac. Others
feel the city should wait until other
nearby communities are ready toI
unite in financing one large treat
ment plant for the entire Northern
Virginia area.


AS result, Alexandria's sewer
plans have been filed away for
nearly two years. There are no
indications that the city plans to
put them to use any time soon.

CLEVELAND. Aug. 15.-"Talk

Steel magazine said today.


Uncertainty clouds the long
term outlook for business" Steel
reported. THE trend over the re-
mainder of the year = hinges
largely on settlements in the cur
rent steel and automotive wage
disputes, especially the former,
which may set the pattern for
most other industries.

more active, but mill order back
logs continue to shrink, the maga-
zine found. It said new business
fell short of outgoing shipments.

manufacturers for steel products
and inventory replenishment have
slightly bolstered "sagging" steel
making operations. Steel said.
adding that several idle open
hearth and electric furnaces were
put back to use last week.

still comes from automotive and
related industries, the magazine
said, warning that it would not
be surprising" if automotive steel
buying were cut next month in
the event that a steel strike is
averted.

have been taking more steel than
they actually need as strike insur-
ance.


Steelmaking, the magazine re-
ported, increased for the third
consecutive week, rising one point
to 825 per cent of capacity, high
est since June.

LONDON, Mar. ia gray
haired Scottish surgeon operated
on King George vi today in the
hope of relieving his serious leg
ailment.


The nine royal doctors who
gathered around an operating
table set up in Buckingham
Palace bedroom reported later the
kings condition was entirely
satisfactory"
A later bulletin tonight said the
king had a restful day" and his
recovery from the operation is
proceeding smoothly"


The operation was brief, but
delicate. The surgeon, Prof. James
r. Learmonth. severed a nerve
near the spine which controls the
tension Of the main artery in the
kings right leg.


For five months King George
has suffered from faulty blood
circulation in the leg that might
have caused gangrene and loss
Of the feet.


BY cutting the nerve-an oper-
alton called lumbar sympathec-
tomy-the doctors hoped to relax
the artery and permit the blood
to flow more freely.


The King was reported rest
ing fairly comfortably a few hours
after the operation. Princess
Elizabeth and Prince Philip left
the palace later in the day-a
sure sign that the royal family
was not worried.


The doctors reported last Tues
day that circulation in the left
leg was improving with treat
ment.


The Kings ailment - called
thrombo angiitis obliterans-was
discovered last November after he
complained that his feet felt
numb.


He has been resting most Of
the time since. A tour OF Aus
tralia and New Zealand by the
royal family this spring was post
poned.

feared to risk transatlantic

cred wheels.

landing position, but the hy-

ate the brakes failed.


Rain had made the Shannon
runways slippery, so he chose to
set down at Heathrow, where the
runWayS are longer.

NANKING, Mar. 1.-National-
ist peace delegates, prepared for
long negotiations on three Of the
Communists eight conditions for
peace, will leave for Peiping to-
morrow.


Delegation Chairman Chang
Cnih- chung said the Communist
demand for punishment of So
called war criminals, army reor-
ganization and formation OF a
coalition government would re-
quire much negotiation.


The other five conditions, cov-
ering restoration of civil liberties
and economic reforms, have been
a part of the governments pro-
gram all along, he said. He added
that the government unfortu-
nately had not gotten around TO
implementing them.


' Chiang's Blessing Reported.
! The delegation, Chang told
Chinese legislators, will go to
Peiping for the peace talks with
the blessing of retired President
Chang Kai-shek. However, po-
litical observers accepted this
statement with tongue in cheek.
Chang has been an 1mplacable
foe of the Reds throughout %
years of civil war. He also heads
their war criminal list.


Likely the world will get little
information about the peace talks
once they start. The Communists
have barred foreign and Chinese
neWsmen. The Red radio, the
only medium disseminating news
from North China. likely will re-
port the peace conference. But
this news of the historic event in
all probability will be slanted to
the Communist view.


Foreign Newsmen Silenced.
Foreign neWsmen in Peiping
have been silenced since February
by the Communists. Applications
to cover the conference have been
made by foreign newsmen in
Shanghai and Marking but no
answer has been received from the
Reds.


The Communist victors in the
long war will call the turn of
events at Peiping. French
educated Chou En-lai will head
the Communist negotiators. His
role will be far different from that
in 1916 when Gen. George Mar
shall tried to bring the National
lists and Communists together. At
that time the Reds were on the
run and Chang Kai-shek was die
tating the terms.

Well. we're really deep in sum-
mer now-and that means fresh
succotash time. There is nothing
to compare with the combined
flavors of freshly picked corn, and
freshly picked baby lima beans.
Even the Indians believed in start
ing them together early-they
planted the bean vine in with the
corn, so that the vines could climb
up the stalks!


The odd name is believed to
come from the Indian IN 'sickqua-
tash" which. roughly. meant whole
corn, not ground. They taught
the Pilgrims how to combine the
corn and beans. and from this
simple beginning developed several
elaborate connections all known
by the same name. This was
especially so in Plymouth, where
succotash meant a dish of large
white beans, hulled corn, corned
beef, salt pork. chicken, white
turnip and potatoes. 1t was the
traditional feast at celebrations OF
Forefathers' Day, on December 81.


Today different localities have
their own versions of succotaSh.
In Maine the beans and corn are
cooked separately, and the corn is
cooked with little salt pork and
sweet cream. The beans are SIM
ply boiled. When combined the
mixture is allowed to simmer five
minutes or so, and then is dressed
with more cream and butter.
New England succotash" doesn't
use lima beans at all. Here shell
beans are combined with the corn
always yellow-and salt pork.
In Connecticut cranberry beans
were chosen. and cooked until
done with salt pork. The corn was
cooked on the ear, then scraped
into the beans, and all salted and
peppered.


The Penn-Dutch version of sue
cotash is more elaborate. 1t con-
tains green peppers, tomatoes. po-
tatoes and brown sugar. as well as
the corn and limas. Chinese sue
cotash, which Is the Pacific Coast
choice. is made with yellow corn
and shell beans, literally favored
with soya sauce. In the South
okra, tomatoes and perhaps onions
may be added.


I must say, especially when the
fresh young vegetables are used.
that I prefer the simpler versions.
cook two cups of baby limas in
salted boiling water until just ten
der. Then I add three cups OF
freshly scraped raw corn kernels.
and let all cook for 10 minutes
no more, and less If the corn and
beans are very young. Then drain
them well. and stir in good bit
Of salt, plenty of freshly ground
black pepper, some butter and
some scalded cream. There should
be just enough to bind" the
beans and corn. and not be too
liquid.

rebels have seized vantage points

More bad weather hit portions
of the storm-stricken Western
rangelands today. Snow and

degree the fight on many fronts
to save the millions of starving
and snowbound cattle and sheep.


There were fresh falls of snow,
accompanied by strong winds, in
Nebraska and in parts of. Nevada,
Utah, Idaho and Arizona.


Nebraska, one of the hardest hit
by the earlier billiards, received
the most snow. Winds whipped it
into drifts over the newly cleared
highways and rail lines and cur
tailed relief work in the disaster
areas.


Lesser Amounts Elsewhere.


Lesser amounts of snow fell in

did not seriously interfere with the
relief operations. And Federal and
State officials joined in the battle
to dig out from the worst winter
weather in several years in the
Western Plains and Rocky Noun
tain region.


Emergency cash relief came from
Federal and State sources to finance
the huge task of saving the more
than 100000 cattle and sheep
which are in varying degrees of dis
stress in the Western storm area.


Moving with record speed, Con-
gress yesterday voted $5O0O00 for
the blizzard-swept area and then
began work ON another appropria-
ton of 100000 for the same pur-
pose.


Senate Approves Fund.


A resolution authorizing this
larger sum passed the Senate, but
must wait until Monday for House
consideration. This resolution, in
addition to permitting appropria-
ton of money specifically for use in
the Western area, also authorizes
reimbursement of Federal agency
funds for money spent in the
month-long fight against the
storms. 1t also would allow the In
dian Bureau to provide food and
fuel for reservation Indians in the
area.


Technically, the $500,000 approved
yesterday goes to President Tru-
mans emergency fund into which
he may dip for quick money needed
for relief in such cases as billiards,
hurricanes. floods, etc. The president
asked Congress for a new 81 ,000, 900
disaster fund yesterday.

also struck over other sections Of
the Nation.


There was widespread precipita-
ton over the central part of the
country. There was a band of
freezing rain and sleet from South
ern Lower Michigan into Texas.

weather picture. Warnings were
issued for 171-mile stretch of the
Ohio past Cincinnati. About 1000
families have been driven from their
homes by flood waters from Ohio

ton.

that the Nationalists had scored

the Nationalist reinforcements
had gone into the Tayu and
6iaomei mountain region along
the north border of Kwangtung
Province. Of which Canton is the
seat. This area faces the town
Of Tayu. which the Reds took two
days ago.

valley 10 miles to the Canton
railway, rather than south into


the hills0


Reports Are Credited.


Numbers of troops passing
through Canton in the past few
days indicated the reinforcement
reports probably were true.

however. Meanwhile, reliable in
dependent sources confirmed gov
ernment reports Of the past cou-
pie Of days that Gen. Pal Chung
hsi's defense forces had defeated

BALTIMORE, Mar. 1.-THE old
German liner Amerika, which
plowed the seas through two
World Wars and for many years
more under the name America, is
headed for the boneyard again.


The Maritime Commission said
today the ship will be laid up at
Hawkins Point, alongside the
George Washington, another for
mer Hamburg-America Line ship.


The Amerika was confiscated
from the German line during
World War I. 1t was converted
into a troop TRANSPORT and after
the war continued in service car
rying passengers under the name
America.


The ship was laid up at Solo
mons Island from 1882 until 1889,
when she again was put in COM
mission.


After complete refitting in l941
the ship was used as a troop
transport between New York and
European ports. In 1916 she was
altered to carry military depend
ents.

traffic bottleneck.


Heinz Bracht. union chairman,
said the union Is not only willing

set up an emergency elevated sys-
tenn.


MIR. Bracht said in the British
licensed Telegraf that the West
Berlin population could mot be
expected to suffer from the ele-
waited situation any longer"


West Berliners now jam the
underground trains, cling onto
autos and trucks or walk.

The union has offered to handle
interzonal trains, but declares the
railway management will not per-
NIT it.


Mr.. Bracht suggested the ele-
waited problem be solved by au-
thorization from the West Berlin
city government to set UP sep
arate service. He reported suf-
ficient coal, power and personnel.


An American spokesman, how
ever. said establishment Of a sep

peals ruled today that the District
will not have to pay the Wake
field Dairy an additional S4.482
for milk purchased for public in
stitutions here in 1946.


The milk was purchased under
a contract which contained an
"escalator clause" to cover any
price changes set by tht Office of
Price Administration which then
was still in existence.


The appellate court held that
the clause, although prepared
while OPA was still in effect,
nevertheless was not binding be-
cause OPA went out of existence
before the contract ended.


The dairy claimed it sustained
losses amounting to $4,482 because
prices the dairy paid to producers
for milk products were increased,
but the District refused to help
absorb the increase by paying
more for its purchases.


The Wakefield attorney, John
F. Hillyard, contended in the suit
that although OPA was suspended
while the escalator clause was in
effect, other existing Government
agencies took over price regula-
ton functions.


Mr.. Hillyard contended that the
PRICE Decontrol ;, Board, and the
Agriculture Department were. .OPA
successors" having power to fix
dairy products prices and that the
escalator clause still was binding.


Chief Judge Harold M. Ste
phens held, however. that the
decontrol board and the Agricul-
ture Department were not "suc-
cessors" to OPA. He further
pointed out that the decontrol
board, acting under powers dele
gated by Congress. refused to
keep the dairy products in ques-
ton under Federal price controls.

The 1uSt-completed washington visit of
high-ranking Icelandic mission headed
by Foreign Minister Benediktsson heralds
another prospective member of the Allan
tic Pact. Small and militarily weak
though it is, Iceland would play an i'm
portant part in the new European -Ameri-
can defense system.


A glance at a map of the North Atlantic
reveals Icelands high strategic impor-
tance. This island lies just north of the
transatlantic great circle" which forms
the main shipping route between North
America and Northern Europe while it Is
likewise on the air route between the two
continents. Its strategic Importance was
abundantly demonstrated during the late
war. At that time, Iceland was linked
to Denmark by allegiance to common
Crown. The Nazi invasion of Denmark
and Norway in the spring of 1910 raised
The threat Of a Nazi descent upon Iceland,
which was entirely defenSeleSs against
invasion because it had neither army nor
navy, its population barely exceeding
100000 widely dispersed over its rugged
and infertile territory.


To. guard against that threat, British
and Canadian forces promptly occupied
Iceland with the acquiescence of the
local authorities Once In possession, the
British proceeded to use Icelandic ports
as naval bases and laid out air fields.
After our entry into the war, American
technical forces took over the air fields,
which were further developed and played
an important part in the aerial patrol
and reconnaissance system which did so
much to guard shipping against the
German submarine campaign.


This wartime occupation had been
coupled with specific promises that it
would be terminated after the end of
hostilities. Accordingly, when the Ice
landic Government requested fulfllment
of this pledge, our technical forces were
withdrawn and the airfields came ,under
Icelandic control. They are now used
purely for commercial purposes But their
strategic value remains.


The Icelandic delegates while here,
made it plain that their Government will
not contemplate the granting of base rights

BERLIN, Oct. lit was taps
for the Berlin Airlift last night.


The last plane of the lift, a
United States Air Force C-54, car
ried news correspondents and coal
from Frankfurt to Berlin. A band
played and the Tempelhof COM
mander, Maj. Gen. John K. Barr
hauled out the last sack of coal
in the plane.


That was the last act in the
15-month life of the airlift. Dur
ing those Is months the Ameri-
cans and the British made more
than 275 900 flights over the Rus
sian blockade into Berlin, carry
ing more than 100000 tons into
the beleaguered city. The air.
lifts success forced the Russians
finally to back down and lift their
blockade.


To the end the operation was a
record breaker. It had been
planned to end October 81. but
airmen kept flying in the food and
supplies at such rate that the
last plane arrived yesterday, a
month ahead of schedule.


In closing down the airlift both
the Americans and the British
said they would maintain training
squadrons in Germany. Repre-
sentatives of both nations said
they could start the aerial supply
again rapidly should it become
necessary.

The Australian coal strike Is over. The
men 60 back to work Monday under a
directive from their leaders. This decision
was inevitable when the union membership
voted decisively to end the strike, despite
the recommendation of the leaders to hold
out. Thus ends what was probably the
gravest challenge to constituted authority
which the Commonwealth has ever faced.


This was no ordinary strike. Illegal
from the start, 1t developed into test OF
strength between the government and a
Communicated labor organization occupy
ing key position in the nations economy
Furthermore, the miners we're backed by
other radical unions such as the long
shoremen's and seamens organizations,
who staged sympathetic strikes and added
to the economic confusion which the
miners had precipitated. The political
nature of this contest became doubly obvi-
GUS when the government raided the head
quarters Of the Australian Communist
Party and obtained evidence that the
whole business had been ir1stigated from
Moscow. The party leaders are about to
be indicted by the Commonwealth on sedi-
tion and conspiracy charges.


The government acted vigorously to
combat this quasi-revolutionary challenge.
When the miners union officials def1ed q
court order enjoining them from using
union funds for strike benefits, they we're
promptly jailed for contempt together with
officials of other unions who had illegally
donated funds for the same purpose. These
arrests further sharpened the issue, the
strikers vowing they would not return to
work until their leaders were freed and
all fines remitted. Meanwhile, the strike
itself, timed at the depth of the Australian
winter when coal stocks we're abnormally
low, was literally disrupting the nations
economic life. Industry was half paralyzed,
essential public services slowed down, and
city dwellers were subjected to severe hard
ship from unheated homes and lack of
cooking facilities. To meet that crisis the
government sent troops into the coal fields
to mine coal and insure its distribution.


ALI this took political courage and in
volved definite risks. 1t should be renem-
bered that the present government Is
Labor administration and that Australia
is strongly unionized. The radical unions
did their best to infame labor senti-
ment generally against the governments
strike breaking" measures, hoping to pre-
cipitate something like q general strike
and what Communists term a "prerev-
olutionary situation" But the group OF
Communicated unions found themselves
isolated. The bulk Of organized labor either
tacitly or openly approved the govern
ment's actions. Hence, the rapid cave-in
Of resistance, when the union rank and
file could not be held in line and the
leadership had to capitulate.


From this outcome several consequences
can be deduced. The setback to the
ultraradical section of organized labor is
obvious, and there is q fair chance that
Communist leadership may be ousted from
control by the disillusioned members OF
those unions. The government is propor-
tionately strengthened, not only from en-
HANGED prestige with the general public but
by proof that the majority of organized
labor Ii sane and sound. The showdown
thus served useful purposes and was worth
while from an overall viewpoint.


Yet the cost has been as heavy as 1t was
economically needless. The strike losses
probably run well over 5000, 900, more
than 100000 workers were made idle and
the industrial disorgsriization has been so
great that 1t will be some time before full
production can be resumed. This has
been q costly business. It is to be hoped
that the lesson has been well learned.

nese Communists gave signs to-
day of getting ready to invade the

Chusan, $50 miles down the coast
from Red-occupied Shanghai.

Chen vi has mustered a large

jective is to knock out the base

ri has moved his field headquar-

shek's native city. less than 40

commanders, alarmed at the fall

eminent agencies were told to
evacuate to make room for the
troops.

ming Post said over 10000 Ma

CHEYENNE. Wyo.. Oct. 10
Forced off its regular route by
storms, Slick Airways cargo
plane crashed last night near
Cheyenne Airport, killing its three
crewmen.


The San Francisco-to-Denver
twin-engine plane nicked a knoll
three miles northwest of the
Cheyenne runways while coming
in for a landing. The plane had
been directed to land here rather
than at Denver where rain and
fog limited visibility.


The C-46 craft skidded across
rough terrain for more than city
block before disintegrating into
tangled mass. There was a light
mist but visibility was satisfac-
tory.


First reports were that four had
been killed. Coroner Wesley
Schrader said an embalmed body
that was part Of the cargo had
been mistaken for a passenger.

WILMINGTON, Del. Oct. o.
Two Of eight convicts who es-
capped from the New Castle
County workhouse were behind
bars again today. but their six
heavily armed companions re-
main at large.


John Henry Minor. %. Bear
Cleve, Fla, and Jesse w. Palmer,
%, Tuscumbia, Ala, both Negroes.
were captured last night after
wild highway chase which ended
when their stolen yellow convert
ible overturned on U. S. Route 40
near North East, Md.


Still clad in their prison garb,
the two men leaped unhurt from
the damaged car and tried to flee
on foot. They were stopped by
State police without shot being
fired.


Manhunt Intensified.


Their capture served to inten-
sify the manhunt for their six
accomplices in the daring prison
break Wednesday night.


The eight locked two guards in
q cell, took pistols, rifles and am
munition from the prison arsenal,
and used a third guard for a
human shield as they marched to
freedom through the main gate.


Minor was serving a life term
for murder and Palmer was serv-
ing IL years for robbery.


Those still at liberty are:


Danny Norris. 20, Of Whining
ton, serving a life term for Staying
Wilmington Detective Thomas
Conaty; Joseph Lankford, rs, Bel
lefonte, Del, 10 years for robbery;
Willie Edwards, %, Satsuma, Ala.
one year for obtaining money un-
der false pretenses and three years
for . prison break; Victor Bryson.
20, Minquadale. DEL. three years
for robbery; Edward Ernst, rs.
Wilmington, four years for rob-
berry. and Edward J. Hardy. 23.
Gloucester, Mass, six months for
breaking and entering.


Spotted Stolen Car.


Delaware State police began the
chase after Minor and Palmer
when they spotted the car re-
ported stolen from Lawrence
Smith of Landenberg, Pa.


MIR. Smith said the two men
held him up In his workshop. They
took his watch and a small
amount of money. forced him to
get the car keys from the house
and tied him up before driving
OF. Mrs. Smith, who hid In the
house during the holdup. tele-
phoned police.


The alarm was relayed by
Pennsylvania authorities and Del
aware troopers sighted the car
near the Maryland-Delaware line.
The car was forced to the side Of
the road and overturned as Mary
land police joined the chase.


Minor and Palmer as well as the
six still sought were described as
hardened criminals who would
shoot to kill" At least two Of the
fugitives are known to have made
their original escape in stolen
automobile found aban-
doned in Kennett Square, Pa.


This coupled with last nights
chase led police to place renewed
emphasis on the roadblocks
thrown up shortly after the escape
Wednesday.

Mans dependence upon nature has again


been exempliied in a recent statement


from w. Averell Hartman, Marshall Plan


Ambassador to Europe. Returning to this


country from an investigatory visit, he


expressed concern over the possibility of


poor grain crops In much of Europe owing


to the current drought there. The situa-


tion is not yet critical, but abundant spring


rains are imperatively needed in order to


insure normal harvests. Unfavorable con-


ditions are widespread. ranging from


France and Portugal to Romania and


Southern Russia.


Drought In Eastern Europe is no novelty,


because 1t has continental climate some


what similar to our own, with dry periods


that can cause acute crop shortages
Western and Central Europe. however, are
normally more favored. This Is because
their weather tends to come from the
westward, the prevailing winds blowing
loff the Atlantic Ocean, which charges them
with moisture that insures adequate rain
fall This precipitation is naturally most
abundant in the adjacent land areas
Indeed. the British Isles and the north
western portions of the continent often
have excessive rainfall which Injuries the
crop cycle, from planting to harvesting
This was what happened two years ago,
when an exceptionally cold and stormy
winter was prolonged by heavy spring


precipitation. Last year, conditions were
ideal throughout Western and Central
Europe, resulting in almost record harvests
The current trouble began because of a
winter which, though exceptionally mild,
was correspondingly dry. The result is
that the subsoil is badly In need Of moisture
for the crucial growing period. Abundant
spring rains can alone insure proper crop
development.


There are, to be sure, certain mitigating
factors. Postwar agricultural recovery has
reached point where seed, fertilizer and
manpower are again available, while short
lages In draft power and farm machinery
ARE no longer acute. Those were the
shandicaps which plagued European agri-
.culture during the immediate postwar
years. With anything like normal climatic
conditions, good haryests would again be
assured.

sets avenue bridge was discussed and

Seven Robert Gilyard
and his mother are back home
today after spending "a hours in a
Jail cell hurriedly equipped with
crib and diapers.


It all began last Wednesday
when Judge G. G. Parry sentenced
Mrs. Lillian Gilyard, 3S-year-old
mother of nine, to four months in
county jail for Illegally accepting
relief checks totaling $587.70.


The State charged she had
earned that amount working as a
domestic and waitress while re-
ceiving $4,000 in relief payments
over a 21a-year period. The law
requires that any money earned
must be deducted from relief
benefits.


Hundreds Phone Protest.


Mrs. Gilyard appeared before
the 75-year-old jurist carrying
Robert wrapped in pink blanket.
After sentence had been pro-
nounced. some one asked what
about the baby?" .


Judge Parry. reminded Of a
State law which prohibits sepa-
rating mother and nursing child,
ordered the infant sent to jail,
too.


When the story was published
in newspapers. hundreds of per-
sons telephoned City Hall to pro-
test Judge Parry's action.


A group Of civic and business
leaders raised the $587.70; and
Judge Parry agreed to reconsider
the sentence.


In 10-minute courtroom ses-
sion yesterday, the jurist freed
Mrs. Gilyard but warned her she
would be sentenced to two years
in Jail if ever arrested on similar
charges.


Judge Parry told the woman
she was being released through
the kindness of your friends and
the liberality of some other char
liable persons who. I hope. have
not been misled as to your char
acter."


Had Time to Make Good.
The jurist told the woman her
own testimony was:


That, as young Negro girl, !
you came from the State of South
Carolina to Pennsylvania a num-
ber of years ago; that you had had
10 children; that you had never
been married; that the individual
with whom you had lived at the
time your four youngest children
were born, had disappeared and
you did not know where he was"


He said also that he had given
the woman time to make good
the fraud, but that she had not
repaid the sum and that there
fore he fixed the sentence.


Since then, he added. he has
learned she worked the same
fraud" nearly four years ago and
was released upon your written
agreement to abstain from such
practices in the future. Had
I known this yesterday I should
have imposed a more severe SEN

TMERE was the perfect summer day. There
Il was the sweep of green grass, with palm
trees reaching for a blue Florida sky. There
was the shell-shaped pool, flower bordered,
secluded, different except for the standard
bright chairs and big umbrella.


And there was Priscilla! She reclined in
blue chair in a yellow bathing suit, reading.
really reading for there wasn't camera
within sixty miles. For once!


Priscilla had to be seen to be believed Not
that she wasn't seen, constantly. A hundred
million Americans saw Priscilla, from bill
boards magazine covers, advertisements and
fashion show runways. Her beauty was as
widely publicized as Gromyko's mo" and far
more pleasing to the eye five feet ten, aged
nineteen, size eighteen shoulders, twenty-three
waist golden-brown skin, violet eyes, tawny
hair bleached only by the sun.


Today her public numbered two. They
stood, arm in arm, on the terrace overlooking
the pool, schoolmates recently reunited after
twenty years of separation: Sarah Rutherford.
who owned the low-roofed. smiling house and
the visible landscape; and Louisa Jaynes. of
East Sixty-third Street, Manhattan, who was
chaperoning her niece, Priscilla, on mod
cling expedition to Florida.


1t was about to happen. the thing they had
schemed for, dreamed about and prayed over
since their reunion. Priscilla was about to
meet Sarah Rutherfords aviator son Jack
Ensign: US.N., now stationed at Pensacola
They would meet and fall in love, two young
people obviously made for each other When
the two women saw a long blue convertible
turn into the driveway, they clutched hands
like guilty schoolgirls and disappeared into
the house.


Priscilla also heard the car, but did not turn
her head Minutes later. when shadow
passed between her and the sun. she turned
a page, counted slowly to ten and looked up.
If she gave an involuntary start. she concealed
it by dropping her magazine.


Jack Rutherford, in bathing shorts and
robe, didn't pick it up. He merely said, How
will you have me, down on one knee, or flat
on my face at your feet?"


Priscilla studied him dehantly. Six feet
two, dark, broad d-shouldered. slim, self-assured
with blend of airman's arrogance and Navy
poise.. His gray eyes could chill at glance
and at the moment the chill was on.


She rose slowly. advanced two steps, placed
her arms carefully around his neck. said,
MY heror' in a very fiat voice, and kissed
him languishingly full on the lips. As she
released him Jack staggered slightly Priscilla
went back to her chair, picked up the maga-
zine and went on reading.


Jack walked to the diving board, struck
the water smoothly, SWAN twice the length OF
the pool and then pulled himself up dripping
on the ledge nearest Priscilla's feet.


Been in?" he asked.

public buildings. The press was
under strict censorship. But with

normally yesterday.

Polish point of view, 1t comes as the

signed recently between Poland and coun-

of these being with Argentina


Economically speaking, this notable
extension of Polish trade relations with
the Western world implies a relative
diminution of its commercial dependence
upon the Soviet Union and its satellites
But the mere fact of this extension has
significant political connotations. Such
trade agreements could hardly have been
made by Polish government VIGOROUSLY
subservient to Moscow unless Moscow had
given its assent. And that, in turn
suggests that the Soviet Union has been
unable to fill the gap in Western trade
which opened when Poland, under Soviet
pressure, opposed the Marshall Plan and
cut itself off from the contingent benefits
1t might have gained by adhesion thereto


Another interesting feature of the
agreement is the fact that the British
negotiators have been able to drive
favorable bargain on reimbursement for
British property nationalized by Poland's
communlstic regime. Britain has insisted
on compensation for such property in trade
negotiations, not only with Poland but
also with other communistic governments.
such as Yugoslavia, which have similarly
nationalized foreign holdings The British
claims against Poland for compensation
aggregate some 100000 sterling. Under
the projected treaty, Poland is believed to
have agreed to settle on basis of between
25,oOO,oOO and 100000 sterling, with pay
ments to be spread over fifteen to twenty
years. That is certainly better than we
have done. About $500 100000 worth of
American property in Poland has been
nationalized, but American claims have
begged down in the Polish courts, with
little apparent chance of settlement that
would prove satisfactory to the American
owners.

most of the population remaining

Canton -Hankow railroad to within
30 miles of Canton. There was no

To the Editor Of The Star:


Today, October %, marks the ninth ami
versary Of Greece's entry to the second World
War at the side of the Western democracies
This observance comedies with current vic
tories Of Greek armed forces over the Com
munist rebellion of the past five years, in
Spired and armed from abroad. At this
anniversary, the Greek people dare to hope
for the first time that warfare finally Is
ended.


Fully aware Of the great moral force that
helped shape victory over lawlessness and
disorder and appreciative of sympathetic
understandings from the free and civilized
democracies of the world, they now con-
f1dently look to the pursuit of such peace
full occupations as rebuilding their nation
physically and economically.


While continuing constant vigil to safe
guard their borders from such fresh dangers
as may emanate from abroad, the Greek
people now will begin realizing their great
national dream Of fashioning model pro-
gressive democracy among the Red-satellite
countries Of the Middle East and the
Balkans; those dual vital aims now con-
stitute their main concern.


A new generation of Greeks has matured
in the past nine years Of strife and turmoil
a generation thoroughly cognizant of the
vast American aid program which has
made victory possible and peace a reality.
This generation looks for continuing CO.
operation with all the democratic peoples
Of the world but especially to ever-strength-
ening ties of understanding and friendship
with that greatest democracy of all - the
United States.


ANTHONY ANTONAKAKIS.

of Information.

New York today, despite five-day

immobilized ships in this and
other Italian ports. Aboard were
Conductor Arturo Toscanini and
his wife.

the only rift in the ranks of some
1000 striking Italian seamen, who
claim their relief benefits have not
been paid. The Federation of Sea
Workers here said it received a
letter from the Cosulich Shipping
Co., operators OF the Atlantic,
saying it was ready to meet union
demands.


In Naples, some 1000 passengers,
most bound for the United States,
await the arrival of ships. Among
the ships strickbound at Genoa
are the Vulcania, the Amerigo
Vespucci, the Castelbianco and
the Sestriere. The American Ex-
port Line said the Saturnia would
dock here tomorrow after bypass
ing Naples, where it had been
scheduled today.


In Rome, efforts to settle the
strike begged down.

The recurrent Sunday Only" strike Of
locomotive crews on British railways in
wolves several important angles in Britain's
labor situation. Besides the specific points
at issue, the strike, together with the Wild
cat strike by dock workers, appears to be
symptomatic of growing dissatisfaction
and unrest among the labor rank-and-file.


The immediate cause Of the walkout by
the engineers and nremen was the pro-
posed reintroduction of work schedules
under which locomotive operators have to
spend occasional nights away from home.
Behind this relatively minor grievance,
however, are demands for increased wages
and improved working conditions which
have been under negotiation between the
union leaders and railway management.
The unauthorized action of the operatives
in pulling this Sunday strike complicates
those prior negotiations.


Even more significant Is the fact that
the railways have been nationalized. So,
in q sense, the men are striking against
the government, the railway managers
being officials acting In accordance with
directives from above. This is not the
first time that labor has struck in the





have been pulled In the coal mines, which
are likewise national property. The work.
ers, in all such cases, apparently had the
idea that government ownership meant
less resistance to their demands, especially
under q Labor administration. But the
government feels the necessity Of running
the nationalized industries according to
business principles and therefore instructs
management to reject labor demands
which would involve heavy deficits and
lessened efficiency.


Behind this again looms q disturbing
factor which applies to all labor, whether
In nationalized industries or those still
under private management and ownership.
That Is the growing gap between wage
scales and the cost Of living. The pur-
chasing power Of the pound sterling is
dropping, and the workers are consequently
impelled to demand wage increases sufii-
cient to make up the deficiency. But any
general increase In wages. to say nothing
Of concurrent labor demands for easier
working conditions, would have dis
astrous effect upon Britain's export trade,
on which It's very economic life depends.
British goods are being literally priced out
OF the world market because they cannot
compete with goods produced more cheaply
elsewhere. The national interest thus re-
quires that prices on exports be lowered
rather than raised.


Nevertheless, although all this has
created considerable dissatisfaction In the
workers ranks and among the British
people at large, this weeks annual Labor
Party conference ut Blackpool has shown

CARACAS, Venezuela. Nov. S.
Homeless Venezuelans searched
frantically today for members of
their families missing since a
flash flood swept through Caracas
suburbs.


At least 20 persons were re-
| ported dead and authorities feared
the toll from yesterdays food
might run much higher. The flood,
the worst in Venezuela's capital in
many years, caused damage esti-
mated unofticially at $10,000,000.
1t was Latin Americas second
major flood since October |.
Heavy rains and floods in Guate-
mala during the first three weeks
of October killed more than 500
persons and caused an estimated
$50, 100000 of damage.


Set Of by Six Hour Downpour.
A six-hour dewnpour yesterday
brought a sudden rush of water
here from the usually tiny Guaire
River, which alresdy was swollen
by several days of heavy rains.


Roaring flood waters swept first
through the crude huts of hun
dreds of poor families living along
the river banks. Radio patrol
cars dashed along the river, warn
ing dwellers on the banks to flee.
Many of the hundreds left home
less said they thought the warn
ing was trick to dislodge them
from their homes.


Whole Families in Water.


Horrified onlookers saw whole
families bob by in the water. help
less amid the wreckage of their
houses and furniture. Eyewit-
nesses said they counted at least
80 men, women and children.
struggling or unconscious in the
flood waters. The floods spread
also to Ell Paraiso, Ell Conde. and
other fashionable Caracas sub
urbs. The waters washed away
the foundations of five bridges.
A number of commercial houses
and storage garages near the
river were flooded.


At the race track near the river,
stables were flooded. Nine race
horses were drowned and IL
others injured. There was an
unconf1rmed report that Caiman,
champion of the current season.
was among those drowned.

LONDON, July 1.-the Labor
government. with almost unani-
nous approval from Parliament
for its broad emergency powers.
sent doubled force Of servicemen
to work today on the strikebound
London docks.


Forty-five hundred soldiers and
sailors, as against 1900 yesterday.
moved into the port area to unload
food ships tied up by the 1S-day
stoppage. Another 2,700 men we're
ordered by the Royal Air Force to
stand by for duty tomorrow.


The Dock Labor Board said
14,204 men were idle today, 3,464
more than when the emergency
was proclaimed by King George WI
at the request of the cabinet last
Monday.


Dock Crews Work 40 Ships.


Work on 1872 ships was held up.
Eight others were being unloaded
or loaded by undermined crews.
Almost 40 ships still were being
worked by full dock crews.


The House of Commons last
night approved the emergency
powers assumed by the govern
ment, which has seized control Of
the dock area along the Thames
River under regulations which
virtually mean martial law. Com
mons approved the regulations by
a vote of 412 to 4. One Co~mu-
mist and three members expelled
from the Labor Party cast the only
dissenting votes.


The emergency proclamation.
first since the general strike Of
1926, is valid for week. Parlia-
ment can extend it to month.


Prime Minister Attlee told
Commons the government would
not tolerate dictation by Com
munists and fellow travellers" He
called for a finish fight with the
strike leaders.


The Executive Committees of
the Stevedore's and Tugmen's
Unions, whose members are idle.
waited for a report today from
union leaders who looked into the
basic dispute yesterday.


There were indications they
might ask the men to go back to
work. but the workers have ig-.
nored similar pleas before from
both union and government off,
cials. The strikers have remained
defiant in the face of government
charges that their walkout is
nist-inspired.
The British union leaders met
yesterday with Canadian High
Commissioner Dana Wilgress, who
had a hand in negotiations to
settle the jurisdictional dispute
between two Canadian unions
which has provoked the London
trouble.


The longshoremen have refused
to unload the Canadian ships
struck by the leftist Canadian
Seamen's Union. The Dock Board
then refused to allow these men
to work other vessels Other dock
workers struck in sympathy.


The strikers say they are fol-
lowing trade union principles in
refusing to work "scab" ships.


In radio speech last night.
Labor Minister George Isaacs
said the ships were not scab be-
cause the Canadian Trades and
Labor Congress had held the
c. s. U. strike political.

The aircraft of two American

Smith and Sergt. Bender were well
treated by the Communists and
that he was writing missionary
friends in China to do what they
can towards obtaining the release
of the two men.


Their wives, Mrs. Smith here
and Mrs. Bender, now in Chicago,
have not heard directly from their
husbands since they were captured.
Mrs. Smith said recently she and
Mrs. Bender planned to stage a
"sitdown' in Washington until the
Government does something about
getting their husbands released.


Senator Knowland. Republican,
of California, visited Mrs. Smith
today and told newsmen that he
favors blockading Chinese Com
munist ports as a means OF apply
ing pressure for the release of all
Americans held by the Commu-
nists against their will.


Senator Knowland said he will
take the matter up with State De-
partment. The Senator recently
returned from trip to the Orient.

with her and Mrs. Bender has

Referring to the editorial Railroad Revo-

For the next 20 years they will be retreating

The. American railway system prior to
WorN War I was stockholders paradise
wherein the manufacture and sale of stock
was more lucrative undertaking than the
sale of transportation. These worthless rode
roughshod over the engineers, who repeatedly
pointed out the fact that most of the mileage
should be relocated and transformed from
pick -and-shovel construction, inducing sharp
curves heavy grades and rough track. Labor
was abundant and cheap, and permanent
rehabilitation should have been made. The
brokers in general were not interested, little
improvement was made, operating expenses
became higher as business and traffic in
creased. Then labor charges scared, and it
was too late. The First World War ended the
recruiting of cheap labor from the Balkan
states and Japan. New construction and
improvements came to an abrupt end.


Some of our highpowered railroads close
by were renewing annually their ties, rails
and fastenings, worn out every IL months,
but there is no other industry in the United





obsolete mechanical structures and accom-
plished so little permanent improvement as
the railroads. Paradoxically, the men who
knew these defects and could have corrected
them have been discredited. Meanwhile, the
financial and business policies of the rail
systems have been dictated by the officials OF
corporate fduciaries who spent their time
hunting lost pennies in the railroad balance
sheets.


During the depression years the whole
industry sought asylum in the Federal courts.
the lawyers became the intervenors and
operators and negotiators for working cap
ital per RFC-Government credit.


Initiative is dead. The average employe
sucks up the income Of the roads. He has
triple -barreled gun trained on the boss: His
union and arbitration board; unemployment
insurance; United States Retirement Pension
Boald. ~,t


The writer, an old timer, knows the prob
lens realize that the railroad employe, who
never knew the sufferings prior to the 16-

slightest conception of the fact that he Is
killing his goose. He demands more money,
kidding himself into believing that all the
boss has to do is write letter to the ICC.
He bites the boss, the boss bites the public.
Like the coal miners who want two-day
week, the railroad men are hungry for the
same fare. The situation is hopeless.


As see it, the railroad men are sitting on

blow up and ruin them. The boys want gov
ernment ownership They may get it quicker

OTTAWA, Ontario, Feb. 19.-The
change in status of Gander airport
when Newfoundland joins Canada
may cost United States and British
airlines hundreds of thousands of
dollars.


Since Newfoundland now is a
British colony, international agree
ments allow full commercial use
of Gander, both for through trans
Atlantic and short-haul traffic.


But Canada never has exchanged
with other countries complete
commercial la aiding privileges,
called fifth freedom rights. The
Canadian government has notified
interested countries that Canadian
policy will apply to Gander when
Newfoundland becomes the 10th
Canadian province March 81.


Therefore United States, British
and other foreign planes will be
able to use the big airport only as
transit stop for refueling and
servicing unless they. get special
agreements before March 81.
They will not be able to carry
passengers between New York and
Newfoundland. orr Newfoundland

PITTSBURGH, July 8.-Start-
to-work whistles blew at Western
Pennsylvania soft coal mines to-
day-but nobody showed up at
the pits.


Obeying John L. Lewis order to
work only three days a week dur
ing current contract negotiations,
miners stayed at home. They
worked Tuesday. Wednesday and
yesterday. After this week they
are needing the United Mine
Worker presidents edict to work
Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday
and then stop.


Coal operators over the Nation
had said they would post work
orders for a normal work week
despite the Lewis order. They
contend the three week
order probably is illegal on the
grounds it restraints trade.


That's why the whistles shrilled
this morning. Operators are stay
ing on the safe side. They pro-
vided work.


Miners are working under the
contract which expired June 80
in the midst of negotiations for
a new pact. Traditionally the
miners won't work without con-
tract. But Mr.. Lewis issued his
three e-day-a-Week order just in
time to keep the miners on the
job. They're earning slightly
more than $40 a week now in
stead of the former average Of
about $40 for working five days.

agencies.

mental bill. with $3,5O0,0oO for a
temporary Office building at Suit
land. Md, for $500 Census Bureau
workers next year, is pending be-
fore the Senate Appropriations
Committee, after being passed yes
terday by the House.


The new structure would be
built in the area now occupied by
several Federal buildings, includ-
ing one already used for many
years by the Census Bureau. The
new building would supplement it.


The measure includes $4,000
more for the Commission on
Renovation of the White House.
The bill carries no funds for an
Iinter-racial swimming pool in

which was closed last summer

sl75,000 for the purpose. But In

money in testimony before the
Senate Appropriations Committee.


The second supplemental bill
probably will be reported to the
Senate Tuesday or Wednesday
next week.

Famed Shonan Beach drive, built
on sand dunes IS feet high was
washed out in many places by
tides which moved 500 inland.

GALWAY, Ireland. Aug 16.-
Search was pressed today for the

q Transocean airliner which ran

in the dark waters of the Atlantic
off Ireland with So persons aboard.


Forty-nine persons were saved
In a dramatic f1are-lit air-Sea
rescue.


The nine others were killed or
lost trying to escape from the
four-engine Skymaster (C-54
which settled into the water so
gently that survivors said they
were not shaken from their seats.


Meanwhile, a full investigation
of the crash went forward today
with American officials partici-
pating. George Clark of New
York arrived at Shannon Airport
early today to investigate the
disaster for the Civil Aeronautics
Board.


Radi0man Is Drowned.


Eight of the victims were among
At Italian immigrants en- route to
Venezuela from Rome. The ninth
casualty, Radioman Herbert Asbel
of Brooklyn was drowned when
the wreckage knocked him from
the fuselage into the sea.


Most Of the Italian-speaking
passengers followed directions
calmly after Capt. Edward Bussey
set the plane down into the
choppy seas.


But some failed to carry out
instructions and jumped into the
water instead of boarding life
boats" Capt. Bussey said. These
were the people who were lost"


Capt. Bussey, veteran of 40
Atlantic and so Pacific crossings,
dropped the plane into the water
after its fuel was gone. Watching
fishermen said the craft "glided
and settled into the sea like q
swan"

of them were able to return today

STOCKHOLM, Aug. 20. -
Swedish observers generally said
today the Communist labor up
risings in Finland are doomed to
failure because Of bad timing.


Experts here who are in touch
with Finnish developments said
privately that the Communists
began their offensive too late.


The Communist tactics of bor-
ing from within trade unions to
cripple industry with strikes and
discredit the government might
have stood some chance Of sue
cess If the offensive had been
started several years ago, the
Swedish observers figured.


They said there was little like
lihood that Russia would openly
come to the rescue Of the Finnish
Communists in striving for their
apparent ultimate goal Of making
Finland a peoples democracy"
on the Soviet pattern.


Finland Is in the unique position
Of havig the only anti Communist
government on Russia's western
doorstep.


Swedish sources who keep well
posted on Finland viewed the
strikes in vital industries as part
OF broad Cominform scheme to
put Finland under Communist
rule.


Red Strength Diminished.


Among influential newspapers
putting the blame on the Comm
form was Morgon Tidningen,
which publishes the government
viewpoint.

munists struck after their strength
and prestige among the workers
had dwindled considerably. Com
munists have been swept out OF

commanding post in the admin
istration, notably the Ministry OF
Interior, the police forces and the
radio. And all nom Communist
parties have pledged themselves

Wet foreign policy were positive,

emily prepared to go out Of her
way to help push Finland's Mos
cow-trained Communists into
power.


The current trend of Soviet
foreign policy. these experts
added, Is one of cautious maneu-
Vering.

or make definite plans for meeting other
needs, including more schoolroom facili-

of the police, fire, school and other
departments have been met.

by the creation of ten new judgeships for
four courts. The Court of Appeals, District
Court and Municipal Court thus will be
expanded by three judges, each, and n
new judge was provided for the Juvenile
Court, which has been kept going during
the prolonged illness of Judge Fay Bentley
by the loan of judges from the hard
pressed Municipal bench The enlarged
judiciary should bring salutary reduc-
ton in the docket logjams which have
slowed up justice during recent years,
particularly in the civil division of District
Court. And the cause of law enforcement
was promoted further by the launching of
special crime investigation by a House
District subcommittee.


Worth special mention is the legislation
giving school teachers paid sick leave.
This long advocated measure rights a
wrong that has contributed to the diff
culties experienced by school authorities
in recruiting and keeping qualified teach
ers. Heretofore i'll teachers have had to
dig in their own pockets to pay for SUBJ
stitutes-a requirement that was unfair
and that long has been source of irri-
tation among local teachers.


Left for further consideration were such
problems as home rule, District representa-
tion in Congress, the future of the slum
Clearance and Redevelopment Land
Agency and the Sasscer Metropolitan
Area coordination bill. The last-named
measure grows in Importance as the field
Of conflicting governmental activities
grows larger in the fringe communities
around the District. The second session
OF the 81st Congress would be justified in
giving early attention to the problem of
bringing about better coordination of
interarea planning and action throughout
the Greater Washington region.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, July 25.-
While unofficial sources put cas-
ualties much higher in Saturdays
earthquake on the Aegean Coast,
the semi official Anatolia news
agency reported last night that
two persons had been killed and
four seriously injured.


Two more deaths and injury to
48 persons on the Greek island
of Khios, IL miles off thu. Turkish
coast, were reported by the Greek
government in Athens. A Greek
warship with medical aid and
other supplies was sent to the
Aegean island.


The tremors shook Izmir, Tur-
keys second largest port, where
considerable property damage but
no loss of life was reported.


The fact that most of the pop
ulation was kept outdoors be-
cause of excessive heat and many
residents refused to return to
their homes, as the tremors con-
tinued, accounted for the COM
paratively few casualties. Some
reports said 400 houses were
damaged or destroyed.

/ Many people just can't abide the
humble parsnip. They may "be
able to eat anything" but they jibe
at the pale root. This article Is
not for them, because it sings the
winter vegetables praises for a
change!


| Parsnips aren't fit to eat until
the frost has touched them and
changed their starch to sugar. Per-
haps some of those who don't like
the root have encountered them be-
fore this chemical transformation.
They should try again.


Parsnips, when growing in the
wild state, are actually poisonous
and UNBEATABLE. No one knows what
brave man brought the first plants
under cultivation. Evidence shows
that parsnips were cultivated widely
by the ancient Greeks and Romans.
The latter served them boiled with
sauce made of mead or honey
wine, which sounds pretty grim.


The plant always has grown wild
in the Western Hemisphere, but the
first of the cultivated variety was
brought here by the early colonists.
In England, parsnips have been
liked more generally than here and
parsnip wine is an old-taShloned
favorite in the country districts.
A popular English recipe is for
parsnips au gratin. Take several
parsnips, wash them we'll and peel
them. If they are old, cut out the
hard "core," after cutting them
lengthwise into four pieces. Plunge
them into cold, calculated water and
boil them until tender-about q OF
an hour, depending on their age.


Use your favorite recipe to make
rich white sauce, we'll seasoned
with pepper, salt, cayenne and
little nutmeg. Put the parsnlps IN
buttered baking dish, sprinkle with
mixture of breadcrumbs and
grated parmesan cheese. Dot with
butter and brown in a hot oven.
These are surely far cry from the
usual version!


Another novelty are parsnip chips.
Scrape or peel dozen or so medium
parsnips and cut off the stem and
tip of each. Cut lengthwise in thin
slices, removing the core. Let the
slices stand in slightly calculated
iced water for at least half an hour.
Then drain them and dry each one
carefully with cloth. Fry in deep
hot fat as you would potato chips
until golden brown.

sand striking railway workers
fought young Communists, cast in

nearly dozen stations of Berlin's
elevated railway today.


Hundreds were injured during
the fighting, which ragged through
the morning. The outbreak shut
off rail shipments to Western Ber-
lin and threatened to force the
city back to the austerity of the
blockade period.


An elevated passenger train was
set ablaze during one melee.
Clothing was torn from women
who got into the fight.


Western Berlin police said Maj
Gen. Pavel Kvashnin, transport
chief of the Soviet zone, was in
suited and threatened by group
of strikers at the Templehof ele-
vated station in the American
sector.


The police said they gave Gen
Kvashnin protection from the
strikers and he was able to drive
away in his staff automobile with

rate, must give the final decision

ed up over whether Seretse
Khama, chief-designate Of the
Bamangwatos, will reign with his
white bride, London typist Ruth
Williams.


Tshekedi Khama, Seretse's
uncle and tribal regent for 20
years, who talked last week about
going into voluntary exile If the
white queen ascends the throne,
got back his fighting spirit. and
summoned a lawyer from Cape
town for legal advice. The lawyer,
Douglas Buchanan, reached Sc
rowe, tribal capital, today.


At a four-day palaver last
week, Tshekedi and 40 minor
chiefs turned thumbs down on
white consort for their chief. But
Seretse, who has been studying
law himself at oxford and Lon
don, rallied 5000 representatives
of his 100000 tribesmen and was
upheld by a voice vote that shook
the surrounding hills.


After the arrival of Mr.. Buch-
anan. Tshekedis followers ex-
pressed belief Seretse had gained
only a snap decision by the tribal
representatives vote, and 1t
might be reversed.

Two bills appropriating money
for Congress itself came up for
expected House approval today
amid some pleas that economy
should begin at home"


One bill carries funds for the
operation of Congress and its
related activities for the fiscal
year starting July /. It's out-of-

carpets for House members and
new swivel chairs and refrigerators

The S62 ,200.705 total is $685., ia

new year. However, $4,000, 900 of
the budget cut represents failure

mittee to include that amount for
new Senate Office building. The
committee said the Senate should
make the decision on that when
the bill gets there.


Extra Clerk Money.


The other bill provides for extra
clerk hire and a $500 communica-
tions expense account annually for
House members. The extra clerk
hire would amount to $4,000 for
each member.


The bill slid through the House
without debate last month and
without an opposing vote during
sparse attendance. Several mem
bers complained later that they
weren't notified that the bill was
coming up. Had they been tipped
off, they said, they would have
objected and thereby blocked ac-
ton.


Their second shot at the bill
was given them by the Senate,
which wrote in minor amendments
and sent the bill back to the
House. The question today was
whether the House would send
the bill to Senate House con-
ference to adjust the differences.


Called Buck Passing.

down on proposals of some Sena-
tors that Congress pass a resolu-

cut all Federal spending next year

Buck passing" said one House
leader. IF Congress wants spend
ing cut S per cent then it should
have the courage to do the cutting
itself"


He said the House might go
along with legislation that would
give the President Power to veto
individual items in blanket ap-
preparation bills. The President
now has no such power.

defendants in Bulgaria's spy trial
asked the court for mercy today,
but the principal defendant, for
mer Vice Premier Traicho Kostov,
repeated his denial of some of the
charges.


A murmur ran through the
spectators as Kostov spoke, drown
ing out much of what he said. He
spoke after his own defense at
torney conceded Kostov's guilt and

having broken "the hands of the
traitors"

White haired Luben Dukmed-
jiev, one of Sofas outstanding
lawyers, said he could find little
basis on which to defend the for
mer No. 2 Bulgarian Communist.


my task as defense lawyer for
Traicho Kostov is quite difficult, p"

ecution and the lawyers had a
common task Ito find out the
truth


He said. however. that there was
a gap on the accused bench where

with his interior minister, Alexan-
der Rankovic, Dukmedjiev said.
I'VE see here only the agents of
the Titoists and Anglo-Ameri-
cans" he said, adding that the
"aggressors and Warmongers
should also be there.


Testimony in the trial showed,
the lawyer said, that Bulgaria was
facing a catastrophe which was
stopped, thanks to the vigilance
of the Bulgarian authorities who
uncovered the consplratorS' plot
in time.


Severest Sentence Expected.


Speaking further Of the charges
that were brought out repeatedly
throughout the trial that Tito
plotted with the British and
Americans to take over Bulgaria,
Dukmedjiev told the court its
verdict will be not only against
the defendants but also against
them (Titoists and Anglo -Ameri-
cans)."


This statement indicated that
the defense lawyer expected the
court to hand down the severest
sentence on his client. Yesterday
the prosecution had asked that

What the French would call "lAffaire
Thorez" is not only having intense reper-
cussions within France itself but also pre-
sumably indicates Communist policy else
where in Europe, engineered from Moscow.


Maurice ThoreZ, outstanding Communist
leader in France, made statement several
days ago which, though cannily worded
with an eye to evading legal prosecution,
seems to be an incitement for French
Communists to side actively with the
Soviet Army in case it should enter France
in the course of war between East and
West


Broadly speaking, Thorez was merely
affirming a tenet that has always been
implicit in Communist doctrine. A true
Communist everywhere swears higher
loyalty to the cause Of world revolution
which is incarnated in that Red Father
land, the Soviet Union-the kernel of an
eventual worldwide confederation OF
Soviet Socialist Republics.


Nevertheless, in countries not yet under
Communist domination, this overriding
allegiance hitherto has been seldom openly
stressed. For obvious tactical reasons, it
has been deliberately obScured by evasion
or double talk so as to misead the gen.
eral public and hold marginal fellow
travellers" in line Thorez' fortnight state
ment tears away this mask of hypocrisy
and exposes the genuine Communist for
what he iS-a spiritual alien to his native
land and a potential traitor In case OF
war with the Soviet Union.


Since Communist spokesmen never act
on their own initiative but always under
specific instructions from the Communist
international, run from Moscow, Thorez
provocative pronouncement must denote
an important development in Soviet for
elgn policy. The astute minds in the
Kremlin undoubtedly realized the difficult
ties such an unmaSking would make for
the French "Comrades" already under
heavy fire from their compatriotS and
obviously losing ground in France. The
National Assembly has formally con-
demned Thorez for his statement while
the Queuille government has promised to
take legal action against the Communist
Party for this and other recent provoca-
tions. Nevertheless, the French Commu-
mist high command answers defantly and
is obviously closing its ranks by purge
Of its less resolute members


One reason for such provocative tactics
could be an all-out Red campaign against
Frances formal adhesion to the Atlantic
Pact. Yet provocation is so apt to boomer
ang that other reasons justifying the risk
may lie behind The Thorez affair thus
contains implications of distinctly dis
quieting nature.

STOCKHOLM, Sweden. April
22.-Paul Robeson's concert last
night turned into . political row
The trouble started when the
American Negro baritone sang a
new Russian anthem. The first
verse. sung in Russian. was
greeted quietly. However. when
Robson sang the second verse In
English. which most of the au-
dience understood, the crowd
started a demonstration which for
a time drowned out the singer.


Anti-Communists whistled loud
ly (the Swedish equivalent of
boos) and many left the hall in
protest. Pro Communists an
swered with loud cheers and
frantic applause.


Following the anthem Robeson
stepped to the microphone and
told the audience he could no
longer draw the line between his
art and his political convictions.
He said he wanted universal peace,
but above all peace with the Soviet
Union.


After the concert he said his
political activity had increased
lately. He said the reason was
President Truman's Florida vaca-
ton during the Senate's civil
rights f1libuster.

BERLIN, Feb. 12.-The Rus
slams today choked off land routes
for Swedish Red Cross food ship

another step in the cold war.


Maj. Gen. Alexander Kotikov,
Soviet commander. told the
Swedes that such shipments were
banned to prevent any food enter
ing the blockaded Western sectors.
Only gifts for the Russian sector
will be admitted.


German Communists from the
Soviet zone, in companion step,
called mass meeting for Monday
on the doorstep of the British and
American zones to denounce war
mongers." Whether the object
was to provoke disorders or arouse
interest among West Germans was
not clear.


West Denounced Anew.


The Russian-controlled press in
Eastern Berlin heaped fresh de-
nunciations on the Western pow
'ers, and called on all Germans to
resist Allied control statutes.


THE hour of national resistance
has comet must be a. national
fight to take our fight in our own
hands" said typical blast.


Yet American officials reported
some peace feelers from the Rus
sian side, as accompaniments to
these discordant gestures.


The peace gestures contrasted
strangely with announcement by
Maj. Gen. Alexander Kotikov.
Soviet commandant, that he no
longer would allow Swedish Red
Cross food shipments to cross the
blockade lines. The Swedes had
been sending enough food to pro-
vide an extra meal day to all
malnourished Berlin children 3
to 6 years old.

ish and American sectors. Allied

clash followed an anti-Commu-
mist rally in the British zone last
September.

ported Russian peace overtures
were made through Polish resi-
dents of Berlin.

military governor. said he knew
of no official suggestions for re-
sumption Of four-power govern
ment of Berlin, which the Rus
slams broke up last July /. But
an American political official said
Poles, who clearly were emissaries
from the Russians. suggested re-
Gently that new efforts should be
made to settle the Berlin crisis.


American correspondents. in
vited to a cocktail party given by
Polish Journalists found some
Russian correspondents also were
guests. The Russians proposed a
toast to better understanding
not only in Berlin but through
out the world" The Poles said
later the Russians had asked them
to arrange the meeting.
