BUENOS AIRES, Oct. IA
resort-bound passenger train
crashed into a freight just outside
the big President Peron terminal
her late last ngiht, killing about
Is persons and injuring about 100.


A police communique announced
18 dead and Sc injured were iden-
titled, but admitted these figures
Jagged far behind the full toll.


The accident, the worst since
train services were nationalized
two years ago. occurred on the
Gen. Bartolome Mitre line, a half
mile out of the Peron terminal.


Most of the casualties were in
the second class sections of the
passenger train, which took the
full brunt of the collision. Many
of the first class section, however,
were slightly injured.


President Juan D. Peron and
his wife, Evita, and cabinet minis
ters hurried to the scene.


The passenger train, bound for
the summer resort of Tigre. had
left its station seven minutes be-
hind schedule. The freight was
coming into Buenos Aires from
suburban Evita Station.


Wreckage was strewn over the
tracks, and despite night-lone
operations by wrecking crews and
rescue workers, service on the line
Was seriously disrupted. .

ton moves are planned. The leu

government decreed that 10000

leu. The official rate now sets
100 leu as equivalent to 81 United

PARIS, Nov. 25-France two
biggest labor unions called a "a
hour general strike today. but the
demonstration for higher wages
failed to shut down French eco
nomic life completely.


Transportation was disrupted.
Mines and most big industries
were closed.


But reports from throughout
the country showed that large
groups of workers insisted on stay
ing on the Job. Hundreds OF
thousands Of Frenchmen walked
or rode bicycles in a determined
effort to get to work.


Effects of the strike on normal
life were not very noticeable.


Socialist Cabinet Minister Eu-
gene Thomas. who heads the post
Office, called the strike "fiasco."


Strike Held Satisfactory.


Robert Bothereau, secretary of
the Workers Force-one of the
two striking unions-declared "the
results are very satisfactory"
He added, however. that he could
not yet give any figures on the
number of workers actually on
strike.


Business was conducted as usual
in nearly all retail stores, banks
and Offices, which the unionists
had invited to join in the strike.
Throughout France reports gave
generally the same picture: In
dustrial centers idle and calm;
business as usual elsewhere.


A report from Lille said that in
the heavily industrial north the
strike was 80 per cent effective
among chemical factory workers,
10 per cent among textile workers,
80 per cent among metal workers
and 10 per cent among workers at
the Lille railroad station.


The only incident reported so
far was from Bordeaux where 300
strikers prevented the departure
of train to Spain.


The ports of Cherbourg and
Dunkerque, where the Communist
union is very strong, were almost
completely idle.


2 Ships Leave Cherbourg.


At Marseille two cargo ships
sailed out of port, although the
dockers were in a total strike.
Ships also entered the harbor with
no trouble. Dockers refused to
unload cargo but let passengers
get of.


Interior Ministry sources in Paris
said 40 per cent of the railroad
workers and 6 per cent Of the
city's water department workers
we're on strike. The ministry
hoped to have several Paris sub
way lines operating later in the
day.


Two deputies termed the strike
a failure and claimed it showed
the weakness of the unions hold
on their followers.


Jean Moreau, independent, said
the failure proves once more
that the workers are more reason
able than their labor BOSSES"


Strike Atmosphere Varies.


Andre Collins of the Popular
Republican Movement said "the
strike shows that the labor lead
ers don't have the hold on their
followers that they thought they
had"


In Paris, the strike atmosphere
varied. At the government-own
Renault auto plant pickets were at
every door of some $4,000 employ
es. Labor leaders claimed only
1000 were working.


The feeling around the electric
generating plants was one of ten
sion. Signs on many gates there
claimed the strike vote was 100
per cent. From Paris railway sta
tions, trains began moving about
noon after an eight-hour shut
down.


Paris fashion houses remained
open during the strike, but most
Of them closed their sewing rooms,

BERLIN, Feb. 12.-The Rus.
slams frightened their blockade to.
day to stop the Swedish Red Gross
from supplying food for Western
Berlin's children.


This was disclosed by Western
Allied military commandants, who
announced they were providing
airlift space to fly in % tons OF
Swedish soups and cereals.


The Swedes have been conduct
ing a program of supplemental
feeding here which gave all Ger
man children throughout the city
between the ages of 3 and 6 years
one extra meal per day. The Rus
slams let the shipments come
through from the west by rail and
truck.


Now Maj. Gen. Alexander Koti-
kov, Soviet commandant, has in
formed the Swedes that such
shipments henceforth are prohibi-
ted to prevent any food entering
the blockaded Western Sectors
Only gifts for the Russian sector
will be admitted.


German Communists in Berlin
announced today they will hold a
mass meeting Monday in down.
town Potsdamer Platz to denounce
war mongers.


The spot they have selected i:
where the Russian sector border:
on the United States and British
sectors of the city. The announce.
ment of the meeting pointedly ad.
vertised that it was to be ION the
sector borders"


It was not clear whether the
Communists hoped to attract at.
tendance from anti-Communist
Western Berlin or whether they
might seek to provoke disorders.


British and American author
tiles have forbidden Western Ber-
liners to stake mass meetings OF
demonstrations near the sector
borders since the bloody clash last
September at the Brandenburg
Gate after an anti-Communist
rally.


Western Berlin police said they
would watch the Potsdamer Plat2
situation and determine on Mon
day whether extra precautions
would be necessary.

The House has rendered a great service

deserving victims of war service.

ROME, July 30.-Italy. first
Axis country to surrender In
World War II, lined up with some
of her former enemies today des-
pite violent opposition from the
country's powerful Communist
minority.


The Italian Senate approved
ratification of the Atlantic Pact
last night. 1851. and by a show
Of hands, authorized the govern
ment specifically to ratify the
alliance with the Western powers.
The Chamber of Deputies has al
ready approved.


The pact, previously ratified by
the United States. Great Britain,
Canada, France. Belgium and
Luxembourg. will go into formal
effect as soon as the Netherlands
completes action. Her Senate is
expected to debate the issue next
week.


81 Senators Absent.


Italy, along with Norway, Por-
tugal, Denmark and Iceland. is
associated with. but not a founder
nation Of, the pact.


There were 81 members of the
Senate absent as the vote on the
historic alliance against aggres-
sion was taken, but the public gall
leries were filled despite the late
hour.


Vittorio Emmanuel Orlando.
Italy's World War premier, voted
against the pact. as did former
Premier Francisco Saverio Nitti.


Under the pact, Italy, largely
disarmed after her defeat in the
last war, hopes for modern
weapons.


However. Premier Alcide de
Gasperi emphasized that Italy
seeks only better, modern equip
ment, not arms or armed forces
exceeding the limit of her peace
treaty.

BERLIN. Aug. 19.-Rrig. Gen
Frank L. Howley. retiring Ameri-
can commandant for Berlin, said
last night that the Russians are
trying to regain their veto power
in the running of Berlin.
A four-hour session of the city
four military chiefs was held yes
terday, their third meeting since
Paris directive by the Big -Four
foreign ministers last June called
for four-power meetings here.
The directive was issued in an at
tempt to get things back to
normal in Berlin.


Gen. Howley told a press con-
ference later that the Russians
are attempting to revive the old
Allied Kommandatura made up
of the military commanders
which was set up soon after the
war to govern Berlin. Many East
West clashes developed in the
Kommandatura. frequently re-
sulting in stalemates over i'm
portant issues. AS result
Kommandatura sessions became
less frequent, and Russia for
mally withdrew from four-power
rule July /. 1948.


Since then the four occupation
powers have been administering
their respective sectors. with close
cooperation among the three
Western areas.


Referring to our-poWer meet
ings since the Paris directive, Gen.
Howley said:


THE Russians are doing every
thing they can to set up machin-
cry at these meetings which would
turn us back into Kommanda-
tura. The Russians want the
Kommandatura so they can have
the veto power that goes with it."


Gen. Howley expressed belief
that the Russians want to con-
vert the four-power meetings into
a Kommandatura for another
reason-to confuse the people
again. to give the appearance that
the Western Allies are sharing
responsibility for what the Rus
slams are doing in the east zone
and sector"

secretary to the defense attorneys
in the Nick De John murder case.


Captain of Inspectors James
English announced his belief it
was prank after investigating
and comforting with the secretary's
father, Mike Riordan, assistant

San Francisco police chief.


Both Inspector English and Mr..
Riordan said they believed Miss
Rlordan's story of the Saturday
night abduction, but held that it
had no sinister connection with
the De John murder trial.


Inspector English added that the
motive was "incomprehensible."


Miss Riordan. secretary in the
Offices of James Purcell and Will
liam E. Ferriter, said she was kid
naped and held for about two
hours by three men who jumped
into her car.


She said they made her take off
her shoes and drive into Golden
Gate Park, where she was ques-
toned about the murder case, the
attorneys families and the activ-
tiles of her father. who was in
Chicago at the time.


One of the men held a shoe in
his hand and batted her lightly in
the forehead with it, she said.

charges of numbering De John.
former Chicago gangster. was
showed into the background for
most Of yesterday as police. prose-
cution and defense attorneys con-
ferred with Superior Judge Pres
ton Devine on the alleged kid
naping.

episode was not within the con-
Germ of the trial court and ordered
the case continued.

LONDON. Mar. 16.-Diplomatic
sources. said yesterday that the
British Commonwealth is trying to
forge a stopgap barrier against
Far East communism and hopes
later for United States support of
Ia Pacific defense pact.


Some preliminary talks have
been held between the Common
wealth countries and some inde-
pendent Southeast Asia states.
Commonwealth cabinet ministers
and officials close to British For
eign Secretary Bevin said more
talks will follow.


Diplomatic sources said the.
United States appeared unwilling
now to take on new and expensive
military commitments in the Far
East.


Britain and such Common
wealth countries as Australia hope
ultimately their makeshift plan
will become a full Pacific defense
pact. This act. with American
support. would be linked directly
with the Atlantic Alliance.


U. S. Gets Memorandum.


The sources said Britain recently
sent the United States compre-
hensive memorandum on what
should be done to stop the growth
of communism in the Far East.
They said the memorandum met
with a negative" response.


The informants said the Ameri-
can attitude broadly appeared to
be that Britain. her dominions and
the9 Netherlands could do much
more than they have up to now
in organizing their own defense
of Southeast Asia.


Sir William Strang Of the Brit
ish Foreign Office has just re-
turned from the Far East. An Off
cial source said he stressed to the
British cabinet the need for quick
action.


DominiOnS Consulted.


The cabinet then decided to
consult with the dominionS on
calling conference of Common
wealth premiers and foreign
ministers in the spring. Ennis
saries went out last week to each
dominion to discuss details.


One official said the British
government sees the Far East
crisis in terms of Communist
tide which might sweep over a
region inhabited by 100000. 900
people. This area is bounded by
North China and Indonesia and
includes Malaga and the Burmese
hills.


Countries which would be eligi-
BILE for a broader Pacific defense
pact would include the United
States. France, Holland. India,
Pakistan, Ceylon, Australia. New
Zealand, Burma and Siam.

ade. They were there. it said, to
protect the rights of British mer-
chant ships outside of Chinese
territorial waters.

NEW YORK. Sept. 1s.-The
cheaper British pound sterling
may cause only a trifling furry
back of the Iron Curtain at first.
Russia mostly conducts her world
trade on barter basis. She set
ties balances with her large gold
production.


The official relation between the
Soviet ruble and the British pound
has not yet been changed.
Britain and Russia have a trade
pact under which Soviet grain
and other raw materials move
west and British machcinery and
manufactured goods flow east. This
exchange will be affected only as
world prices for these items seek
a new level.


Russia was a prominent buyer
last year in the Australian wool
markets and Mayalan rubber
marts. The upward price squirt
OF rubber and the uncertainty in
wool prices could affect future
Soviet deals, but so far this year
she has not been very active in
either markets.


The trade relations of Russia
and the United States would moi
be greatly affected, since there has
been no change in the ratio oi
the dollar to the ruble.


Russia's part in world trade
had been relatively modest. Latest
figures show she accounts for only
about 7 per cent of the total OF
the interchange of goods among
nations.


Her satellites also operate
through barter pacts with the
western world, but on the whole
have more active trade relations
with the west than does Russia.
They get machinery and wool
from the British, sell them food
and raw materials.

CHICAGO, Feb. about 80 stu

yesterday by escaping chlorine gas.

from a broken tank in the basement,
spread through the building while
the 1,450 pupils were marching out
in fire drill.


The overcome children and work
ers were revived in neighboring
residences by Fire Department
rescue squads. Some victims were
sent to hospitals near the school on
Chicago,s West Side.


A janitor, Louis Gneich, 80, was
washing a basement room when the
1c0-pound tank of gas, used in puri-
flying water for the school swimming
pool. was knocked over. A nearby
fan picked up the fumes and carried
them into the ventilating system.

SCHIRNDING, Germany, Jan. "a.
American soldiers told today how
they exchanged shots with Czech
border guards.
The blazing skirmish Thursday
has gone to diplomatic levels for set
tlement.


Six constabulary troopers said
they "hit the dirt" when from 100
to $50 shots from the Czech side
of the border whistled by them at
waist level. They said they fred
48 shots in return.


No Americans were hit. Czech
officials said all Czechs also escaped
injury, but some American soldiers
said they thought they saw some
CZechs fall.


Give Account of Gunplay.


While American and Czech diplo-
mats from Prague visited the scene,
soldiers engaged in the action gave
this account of the gunplay:


German border guards were tipped
that truck was going to try to cross
into Czechoslovakia with an illegal
load of ball-bearings from Schwein-
furt.


Six guards were posted near an
earthWork border barrier on a little
used road


A truck hove into view and they
challenged it. The driver continued
on and the German guards fired 80
shots into it. Both occupants were
believed fatally wounded.


The driver tried to SWerve around
the barrier and smashed the truck
into tree. The truck halted with
its tail end just 3 feet inside the
Czech frontier.


Czech guards heard the shooting
and themselves opened fire. The
German guards fired 40 shots In
return.


Czechs Used Submachine Guns.


Six American constabulary troop
ers patrolling in jeeps drove up and
Immediately encountered bullets
from the Czech forces. They dived
for the ground and began shooting
across the border with rifles. Later
they found bullets imbedded at waist
level in trees near them. They said
the Czechs were using submachine
guns.


1t. Francis A. Richter of jackson,
Mich, arrived within 20 minutes
with platoon of 18 men as REIN
forcements. The firing still was
going on.


When the shooting quieted. 1t.
Richter went forward with armed
guards and negotiated truce with
the Czech commander.


They agreed to withdraw their
troops from the immediate vicinity
except for three enlisted men from
each side to guard the truck.


1t. Richters reinforcements had
brought up an armored car, 37-mm.
cannon, 50-caliber machine gun and
three 30-caliber machine guns, but
they were not used.


Czech Armored Car at Scene.


The Czechs also had an armored
car at the scene. At one point it
drove up to the earth barrier and
pointed its muzzle along the road
into the American zone, but 1t did
not fire.


American soldiers estimated to-
day that from 100 to 200 Czechs
were engaged in the skirmish.


They said the Czechs by yesterday
brought up the equivalent of a regi-
ment to point mile or so from
the border.


German guards estimated that
the truck carried bearings worth
200. 900 deutschemarks (s70,000).


Czech officials said during the
truce negotiations the truck driver
and his colleague were dying Of
their wounds.


The truck, covered by a lightly
falling snow, still was unmoved to-
night. It's disposition awaits the
outcome of talks between American
and Czech diplomats.

BERLIN, July 8.-Berlin's sup
ply lines were restored to normal
yesterday for the first time in IA
months of blockade and labor
strife, Allied authorities disclosed.


The railway system has over
come the effects of the five-week
West Berlin strike which nullified
the lifting of the Soviet blockade.


Seventeen loaded freight trains
came into Western Berlin Wednes-
day. This was the pre-blockade
average.


The rail system has been pump
ing a daily average Of 10000 tons
of supplies into the Western Sec
tors ever since last week end.


Trucks, Barges Bring Supplies.


Trucks delivered 27.690 tons
from West Germany to West Ber-
lin last week and canal barges
brought another 23.369 tons.


The Allied airlift is averaging
5000 tons daily. This gives West
Berlin now a round average OF
%, 900 tons daily, which a spokes-
man said permits "a generous
stockpile" for next winter, espe-
cially coal.


Most of the West Berlin rail
strikers are now back on the job.
The Soviet-controlled Reichsbahn
(railway) announced the first pay
checks in West marks will be is
sued today. carrying out the terms
of the strike settlement. The
workers will get so per cent in
West marks and the remainder in
the less valuable Soviet zone East
marks. The East mark payments
will be redeemed by the West
Berlin government for West marks
on a 1-to-1 basis.


Some Strikers Quit.


American Military Government
officials said SOC men and 254
women members of the striking
union have quit the Reichsbahn
since the strike ended. They said
these workers were afraid of re-
prisals. There were $4,000 on
strike.


The union itself said it knew of
no specific repriSal acts against its
members. The Soviet transport
chief, Maj. Gen. Pavel K. Kvash-
min, promised there would be no
punishment meted out to the West
Berliners for striking.

Congress gets a reminder tomor-

appropriations to run the Gov
ernment remains unbroken.


The reminder will be the third
request in two months for pass
age of an emergency measure to
pay thousands Of employees and
keep the big agencies running
normally.


This time congressional leaders
will ask stop-gap financing until
probably the end of August.


Already the delayed appropria-
tions are q month and a half late.
The Senate is the offender. The
House passed all the regular
money bills months ago.


Called Unprecedented.


Caught in a money-bill logjam
when the present fiscal year start
ed July l, Congress first passed q
one-month emergency measure to

ing at their normal rate for one
month.


But when July ended. several
big appropriation bills still were
kicking around on Capitol Hill,
so another emergency" bill had
to be passed. The second stop-gap
resolution continued normal A.
nancing until August is.


Chairman Cannon of the House

have we had such a situation"

appropriation bill and the Inte-
rior Department bill.

A fresh mass of cold air from
Canada sent temperatures tum-
bling to subzero levels in areas OF
the Western storm belt today.


Some snow and strong winds
accompanied the new cold front,
which spread over northern Sec
tions Of storm-stricken Wyoming
and the Dakotas and Southeastern
Nebraska. It pushed southwark
over the North Central States and
sent the mercury downward over
Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and
Kansas.


The colder weather eased flood
threats in the snoW-covered low
lands near Falls City, Nebr., where
several streams had spilled over
their banks.


Snow-fighting operations in
Western North Dakota were ham
pered by the new storm. Planes
ready to carry food for ranchers
and cattle in the snowbound
plains were grounded by the storm.


SubZero readings were reported
today over Montana, the Dakotas
and Northern Minnesota. The
mercury dropped more than 40
degrees from Thursdays tempera-
lures in some areas of the new cold
belt.


Ice. rain, snow and floods
plagued the Pacific Northwest
region. Miles of farm land were
under water from the Willamette
River. swollen by heavy rains and
melting snow. A binding snow
storm hit Portland. Oreg.. after a
warm rain storm. Snow measured
more than 18 feet deep at Timber
line Lodge on Mount Hood in
Oregon, where 43 skiiers have been
marooned for a week. The lodge
reported sufficient food and fuel.


Roads in many parts Of South
western Wyoming still were snow
clogged, but nearly all roads In
the more heavily populated sec
tions Of Utah were open. Haylift
operations continued in South:
western and Central Utah, but the
Air Force finished rescue missions
in Nevada.

further legal action.

rioting which has already caused heavy
loss of life and extensive property damage
in Africa is that it is confined exclusively
to the native African and Asiatic Indian
elements of the South African Union.
Whites or Europeans" as they are termed,
regardless of birthplace or nationality,
have not been involved. So far as is
known, only one white man has been killed,
and he was criminal looter shot by police
seeking to re-establish order.


The trouble started and still centers in
Natal, a province of the Union bordering
the Indian Ocean. But sporadic acts OF
violence have appeared elsewhere, and the
authorities have been alerted wherever
Indians are settled. This indicates that
the friction between Africans and Asiatics
is generalized Indeed, this friction has
long been apparent, although it has not
previously hared into violent hostility.


Natal was the logical seat of the current
explosion, because there the two races are
most in contact and the Indians are most
numerous The East Indians of Natal are
the descendants of indentured laborers
brought in long ago to work the big planta-
tons in that semitropical land. The natives
are mostly Zulus, a proud and warlike
people who still recall the days when their
highly disciplined armies were the terror
of all the surrounding tribes. Although
technically part of Natal Province, Zulu
land is still virtually native reserve"
few whites living there, while the Zulus
retain their tribal organization and
Identity. The Zulus living in the developed
parts of Natal have mostly come there
from their homeland to earn a living.
Many of them work for Indians who have
set up as small shopkeepers, peddlers or
moneylenders, catering almost wholly to
native trade.


In Natal, and wherever else this Asiatie-
African relationship exists, bad blood has
been engendered. The Africans complain
that the Indians exploit them and treat
them with indignity. Such Indian arro-
gance is especially resented because they
enjoy no such respect and prestige as that
which the natives tend to give the Euro
peans. Indeed, the natives consider the
Indians as, in some respects, their interiors
and they are aware that the Europeans
feel the same way toward these Asiatics
mostly descended from low-caste Hindus
Such hostility toward the Indians would
naturally be especially strong among the
proud and militant Zulus.


The East Indians are thus two -pronged
thorn in the body-politic OF the South
African Union. The Europeans, who are
the ruling element in South Africa, do
their best to keep the Indians confined to
Natal and prevent their spreading into
other provinces. These restrictions bitterly
offend the Indians, in which they are sup
ported by their homeland, the result being
strained relations between the Union and
India. The current outbreak of native
hostility toward the Indians reveals the
complex difficulties of race relations in
South Africa. And there seems to be no
easy formula for the solution of those
problems.

the tracks.

under control tonight except for
two points near villages.

10 miles of the city. The smoke
was so thick shops lighted their
display windows, and sidewalk
cafes turned. on their nighttime
illumination.


Some 500 reinforcement troops
were sent into the area to fight
the flames. and $50 firemen with
special equipment were dispatched
from Paris. Appeals were made
for civilians Nto fight the fires.
which have been breaking out in
different places in Southwestern
France for the. past month. A
long drought has aggravated the
situation

NEW YORK, Jan. 10.-Followina
many weeks of slow and spotty ac-
tivity, the cotton textile market de-
veloped some business in volume
during the first week of the new
year as many merchants had fore
cast.


Print cloths, sheetings and broad
cloths sold for delivery through the
first quarter of the year. The four
leaf twill also was in demand and
some houses moved this construc-
ton through April Merchants said
buyers needed goods and felt a pro-
longed decline in gray goods prices
had about run its course.


The wool goods market was steady.
A rise in foreign wool prices to rec
ord highs during the week presaged
continued high cost of materials for
mills.


However, there were bright spots
in the picture. The demand for
Women's wear fabrics continued
good. Merchants felt that special
sales of mems suits now in force in
many stores had substantially re-
duced accumulated inventories. The
outlook for the fall line openings of
Woolens and Worsteds in mems wear
appeared better.


The rayon goods market was
quiet. There was a fair demand for
crepes and gabardines. Rayon lin
lngs moved slowly even though
prices were 6 per cent under those
prevailing in the previous quarter.
Some mills curtailed operations as
the supply of goods finally caught
up with demand.

ROSYTH. Scotland, Oct. 49,
Two tiny tugs won their battle
against a North Sea gale and
pulled the damaged British air.
craft carrier Albion into the pro-
tected Firth of Forth today.


The newly built carrier was
holed on the aft port side yester-
day in a collision with the 2,025-
ton coal-carrying British steamer
Maystone. The Maystone sank
quickly with loss of 20 of her
crew Olga.


For time the gale edged the
18.300-ton Albion out to sea de-
spite the straining of the tugs,
which had been towing her when
the collision occurred.


The gale was dying and the
tugs were making 4 knots up the
Firth this morning. They were
expected to bring the ship into
drydock late today. The vessel,
manned by civilians, is being
brought here to be fitted out. Four
Maystone survivors are aboard.

punishment of war criminals"

point for government peace ne
gotiations. Flu was high on the
Communists war criminal list.
yet evidently has been at least
tentatively accepted into the Red
fold.

Pork prices were up about 5
cents a pound. in some Washing

of beef.
The price boosts came as cooler
weather sharpened the demand
for meat. Most other market
products remained about the same
however, with the prices OF some
fruits and green vegetables slightly
lower, according to a survey OF
dealers.


One large chain said the scent
boost is in pork loin and pork
chops, with 1-to-2-cent increase
in bacon. Hams and sausage re-
manned about the same.


Market analysts said farmers
apparently were holding back
many hogs for feeding to heavier
weights. Market runs so far have
been only slightly bigger than a
year ago, when pork was in short
supply.


Most spokesmen. however. said
they expect retail pork prices to
start tumbling, downward within
the next three weeks. as suppliers
hurry the spring pig crop to mar
ket before the support level starts
seasonally downward October L..


Beef prices also are expected to
start declining soon, the Associ-
ated Press said, reporting that
grass-fed cattle now beginning to
arrive in heavier volume soon will
be competing with the anticipated
flood of pork.


Chairman Thomas of the Sem
ate Agriculture Committee this
week urged a Senate investigation
of what he called "egg-price
manipulation" under the price
support program. He suggested
that the Government send surplus
eggs to areas where retail prices
are high, rather than buying them
from dried-egg professors in
powered form.


The Agriculture Department,
however, said shell eggs used by
the driers are uncandled, ungraded
and unsuitable for consumer use
Ofi1cials said there is no surplus
of good quality shell eggs.


Tht National Industrial Con-
ference Board, meanwhile, said
a survey Of 81 cities showed that
consumers food prices declined

year and the same date this year

attractive blonde wife of one of
them.


Tell Maya to come to see me-"
gasped Leonard Clark, 42-year-
old San Francisco explorer as he
was being treated with oxygen for
a bullet wound in the lung.


He referred to Mrs. Maya Free
man, vivacious Polish wife of his
friend Willard Freeman. 41-year-
old businessman from Bridge
water, Mass.


"Where's Maya? Tell her to
come see me-" said Freeman from
another room in the rundown

Nor did Freeman know that his
business associate, Harold Harris,
As, Shanghai-born British sub

Both Clark and Harris were
house guests in the Freemans'

lated that the shooting with

free-for-all-f1ght. but they did

Mrs. Freeman reported she
found all three in an upstairs bed
room when she arose about 10
am. Thursday. Neighbors, called
by her. said Clark lay in his
underwear on a bed, while Free
man was lying nude on an adjoin-
ing bed. Harris body, clothed
except for shoes. was slumped
against Freeman's bed. Harris
had been shot three times.


Police said there were empty
whiskey bottles in the room and
furniture had been smashed. Mrs.

BERLIN, May 1.-THE Rus

Iron Curtain today, ending their
327-day-old Berlin blockade,
major sore spot of the cold war.


Ground traffic flowed on through

pouring supplies and passengers
into the long-besieged old capital
city from the West for the first

The blockade lifting had all

vinced that at last this phase OF
the cold war was ended. whooped
1t UP In the flag-decked city.


The Russian and Western Allied
military outdid each other in cour-
tesy as the barricades went down
ending the blockade and the Allied
counterblockade. There was a
general display Of good will and
smiling readiness to cut red tape.


But the Western Allies were
taking nothing for granted. Their
amlift, which had made the block
ade a useless Soviet weapon by
flying in the food. fuel and raw
materials needed by West Berlin's
1000, 900 residents. continued fly
ing. 1t is to continue at least 80
days, building stockpile OF sup
plies and giving chance to really
sound out Russian intentions.
Today's flights kept supplies COM
ing in at the usual rate.


Newsmen First to Arrive.


Allied military trains. followed

first into Berlin after the barriers

racing down Hitler's famous
super highway. were the first into

The people, who had been slow

the mood. End of the blockade
means for them the promise OF
fresh foods instead OF the dehy-

enough electric lights in their

caused. 1t means that they can
move between the East and West
sectors of Berlin. free again from
the danger of molestation by the
police. 1t means sense of Sc
curity they have not felt for the
better part of year.


The political splitting Of the
city between East and West re-
mained as deep as ever. however.
Each still has its own police force.
city government, fire department
and other services.


So they closed the schools to-

One of the most interesting develop
ments in the Middle Eastern situation is
the growing understanding between the
Turkish and Syrian governments. A Turk
ish military mission is now in Syria with
a view to improving that couptry's armed
forces. But, from long-range viewpoint,
economic discussions between the two gov
ernments are still more significant. 1t is
understood that plans are being drawn up
for the joint development of their Medi-
terranean littorals.


These adjacent coastal districts form
neglected sector of what has been histori-
cally known as 1.-THE Fertile Crescent"
This is band of territory stretching from
from southern Asia Minor down through
Syria, Lebanon and Palestine almost to the
borders of Egypt. Collectively, this is the
region receiving the seasonal rains from
the Mediterranean Sea. Those rains move
eastward until stopped by mountain ranges
which wiring the moisture from the sea
winds, the lands further on being waterleSS
desert. At some points, as the Lebanon,
the mountains rise almost from the sea
and cut off the rains at the very start. In
Palestine the coastal plain is broader. But
at the great bend between Asia Minor and
Syria the mountains are lower and are
interspersed with fairly extensive plains
and river valleys. In ancient times this
was one of the most fertile and prosperous
parts of the Middle East, supporting fa-
NOUS cities and dense population.


Unfortunately, ages of neglect and mis-
use have reduced the region to poverty and
backwardness Extensive drainage develop
ments are needed to redeem malarious
marsh to former fertility, while roads, rail-
ways and port facilities are required to
bring 1t economically in touch with the
outer world. This is the region which cur
rent Turko-Syrian discussions have espe-
eially in view.


The strategic as well as the economic
significance of these plans is enhanced
by the fact that this neglected region is
the connecting link with Northern Iraq
and its rich oil region of Mosul. The po-
>tential key here is the great river Euphra-
tes, which rises in Eastern Asia Minor,
passes through Eastern Syria, and goes on
southwark into Iraq where it. nears its
twin river Tigris, thus forming historic
Mesopotamia, 1.-THE Land Between the
Rivers" Control of the upper and middle
Euphrates would yield abundant hydro
electric power besides important irrigation
possibilities. The results could greatly
enhance the prosperity and stability of all
three nations, thus forming an effective
buffer to pressure from Soviet Russia.

Mckinley High School


So long ago that intervening
years can scarce be counted. the
air was filled with the music of
happy-voiced children. laughing
at their games. Fair maidens
sang all day and the young men
excelled in sports.


Summer ruled the universe
The trees were always green: the
birds trilled and the sky was as
clear and blue as the quiet waite,
Of the Lake of Beauty. where
dwelt Azora. goddess Of the sum.
mer and beauty.


Crops grew without being plant
ed. The joyous people had but
to gather the food OF their choice
when they wished.


In a small city there dwelt q
beautiful maid. Janice. She was
dissatisfied despite the great
number of good fortunes con-
tinually bestowed upon her.


She complained because she
must harvest her share of food
The food grew without her aid
Why should she have to har-
vest 1t?


The germ Of dissatisfaction was
easily spread. Every one became
guilty of this menace to hap
piness. The children no longer
laughed at their play, but pouted
and brightness on every side
seemed to fade. The maidens, no
longer content with singing. scold-
ed and became cross. The men
snarled ut each other.


The once gay and carefree world
was burdened with gloomy peo-
pie. continually finding fault
Will cVSi yGIllllS.


Viewing the turmoil the world
was in, Azora determined to pun
ish the ungrateful people. The
next day the sun did not drive
his golden chariot across the skies
The people we're frightened. Cold
white fakes then began to fall
Soon the earth was covered with
something never seen before
snow.


Rivers and lakes froze.' The
people huddled together in groups
to keep warm, beseeching Azors
to have mercy on them and allow
the sun to melt the ice anc
snow.


Azora then appeared on eartf
In a binding flash of lightning
and spoke in . voice Of thunder
Long have I given you all that
mortals might DESIRE" she said
save only immortality. Yet you
are ever discontented. Now shall
my judgment be descended upon
you. Hear me!


Each year you shall have sum-
mer for part Of the time. then
shall come storms and snow. Cold
winds shall blow and all plants
shall perish from the earth save
the trees.


Summer will follow close on
his icy heels. bringing the warm
breezes again. Thus only will you
remember your goddess and never
again be ungrateful. I have
spoken"


The repentant people protested.
saying they would surely not for
get. But Azora was true to her
words and to this day the year
is divided. Half the time the
sun shines, the children laugh
and play. and every one is happy.
Then comes the winter, crushing
the plants and the peoples hearts
with his icy, cold fingers. Then
mothers gather their children to
their sides and repeat this tale
Just as I have told 1t. always
warning the children to be thank
full and content rather than COM
planning. lest Azora come again
and. in her wrath. cause the earth
to be clasp in winters cold. frozen
hands forever.

ROME. Mar. 12.-Communist-
led crowds stormed through down.
town Rome for a wild half hour
tonight, shouting protests against
Italy's adherence to the Atlantic
Pact.


Jeep-borne riot police quickly
got the situation in hand and
patrolled the area for hours after
ward, alert for new outbreaks.
Heavy police guards were thrown
around the Chamber of Deputies
and Foreign Ministry buildings.


Shouting Peace, Peace" a
crowd of 300 to 1000 leftist
youths. many wearing flaming red
neckerchiefs, tried to storm into
the Palazzo Chigi, the Foreign
Ministry building. Police welded
clubs freely. Traffic was hope
lessly snarled as jeeps raced
through the area bearing police
with drawn tommyguns.


"Down With" Sforza" Shouted.


One crowd swarmed into the
Piazza Colonna. center of many
Communist led demonstrations,
shouting Down with Sforza." :"
Carlo SforZa, the foreign minister,
led the forces favoring alignment
with the Atlantic nations. Italy's
intention to participate in the At
lantic Pact was announced to the
Chamber of Deputies yesterday.


A stones throw from the Piazza
Colonna, the Chamber of Deputies
was in session in Montecitorio
Palace. There the deputies con-
tinued the bitter debate on the
alliance, with Pietro Nenni, the
prot Communist Socialist, leading
the attack on the government of
Christian Democrat Premier Al
eide de Gasperi.


The entire Communist ana pro-
Communist Socialist representa-
ton rose and cheered when Nenni
mentioned Russia. Then the anti
Communists rose and shouted
amidst the general tumult, "Viva
Italia!" Long Live 1talyD 1t was
some time before Chamber Presi-
dent Giovanni Gronchi could re-
store order.


Nenni, whose party has been
elected from the Socialist inter-
national for refusing to break its
Communist ties, charged that the
Atlantic treaty is IAN effort to de-
stroy the United Nations and the
principle of collective security
He said it would lead to war. The
statement was greeted with jeers
and Kisses.

group of Communists in that city,
headed by Senator Mario Palermo
trooped into the city hall to de-
mand an order of the day against
the Atlantic Pact.

BERLIN, April 2.-The Amer
leans and Russians sent out sur
veying teams today to determine
who controls what in divided
Berlin. The action followed three
boundary disputes last night and
today.


Involved are slivers of land
claimed by both the Americans
and Russians. Surveyors were told
to recheck the boundary between
Soviet-occupied territory and the
American sector.


The disputes stemmed from
sharpened Russian efforts to
tighten their blockade against
Western Berlin by such means as
trenches, road blocks and border
police patrols.


A couple Of dozen German
policemen. at least two Russian
officers and several soldiers, some
representatives of the American
military governments public
safety branch and a number of
agitated German civilians got
into the quarrels. No one was
hurt.


Trench Causes Incident.


The first incident occurred last
night at the border between the
American-occupied borough of
zehlendorf and the surrounding
Soviet occupation zone. There
Communists had dug a trench
across a highway to stop block
ade-running trucks.


Germans on the American side
started filling up the trench.
Russian soldiers arrested two
German shovel-wielders. The ar
rested men called for help from
American military police and the
German police of Western Berlin.


In the argument which fol-
lowed. Americans pulled out maps
which showed the spot was in
American-occupied territory. The
Russians produced maps showing
the opposite.

text:
Two weeks of camping in Prince
William Forest Park ended today
for 72 Washington youngsters who
have heart defects that deny them
normal play.


But there is nothing wrong with
their stomachs, nor their brown
backs, nor their smiling faces,
with eyes as bright as the sun on
the swimming hole.


For in two happy weeks they
have leaerned self-confidence. Liv-
ing. playing. working together.
they forgot to feel apart" They
left the "sidelines" and began to
know that they could pull their
weight in a group. too. in their
own way.


Nine-year-old Bobby Howes.
who has a heart ailment prevent
ing any strenuous exercise, learned
how to shoot a bow and arrow.
He knew he. too, could have a
sport, and it didn't have to- be
football.


Norma johnson, IL, shared her
skill at handicrafts with her
friends. Volley ball and races
didn't seem so important any more.


The children who sreturned
home today benefited from the
first camping project for children
with heart ailments in the Wash
ington area and one of the few in
the country. Denied regular camp
ing because they couldn't keep
up," the youngsters were spon-
sored by the Washington Heart
Association. Funds for their out
ing were donated by the associa-
ton and The Evening Star Sum-
mer Camp Fund. The camps, near
Triangle, Va, were operated es-,
pecially for the group by the Fam
lily Service Associations Summer
Outings Committee: Camp Sun
shine for white children and Camp
Wonderland for colored young
sters.


The special camp program has
proved itself completely, according
to all the officials who watched
the children during their wood

NO MATTER WHAT THE
WEATHER OUTSIDE. you'll
find Spring in your heart the
minute you go down to Center
Market City. For here, under
one roof, you'll find the bountt-
full produce Of a bountiful
countryside.


Stands like those Of John
Vassos, who owns stand 233, are
literally filled with mouth-water-
ing fruits and vegetables. John
used to be at the old Arcade
market at 14th and Park Road,
and many of his customers have
followed him to Center Market
City.


When you see the top quality
produce that John has to offer,
you'll understand why. Temple
and King oranges put you in
the mood for a salad or dessert:
Washington State sends Stark
Delicious apples, Empire grapes
and D'Anjou pears for yummy
concoctions; Calavos from Cali
fornia offer plenty Of ideas for
salads and spreads.


New Orleans is sending up
yams-those delightful accom-
paniments to pork roast. Blue
Valentine beans add color and
goodness to spring menus. John
has plenty of garden onions,
Bermuda onions and garlic to
add taste thrills to salads and
other dishes.


Next time you're in the market,
stop by Johns stand-youll find
dozens of good ideas for pleasing
the family palate.


PORK PRODUCTS-The late
President Franklin D. Roosevelt
used to love the baby lima beans
and fresh pork sausage that the
Fred Weigerts, "Momma" and
"Poppa." produce on their Mary
land farm.


Fare fit for q President can
be yours If you shop at this
stand. The Weigerts specialize
in homemade pork products,
and right now they have plenty
of good, old-fashioned pork
sausage. "Poppa" Weigert grinds
it fresh every day, and it's moth
ing for him to grind six or seven
times on a busy weekend.


Another item you'll find here
is cooked corn beef-it's not the
brisket, it's top round" and
very good, too. The Weigerts
prepare their own hickory smoked
hams, also.


At this stand you'll find cooked
sauerkraut and cooked hominy-
perfect companions for pork
products.


Maybe you're one Of the people
who confuses souse with head
cheese. They are not the same.
Souse has more vinegar than
head cheese. The Weigerts have
both souse and head cheese for
you.


Nothing but home dressed meat
is used in the products you'll find
at this popular stand.


THERE'S A fascinating stand
in the back of the Market, stand
148, Augustus.


We could hardly drag our
selves away the other day when
we found that August has laid in
a stock of small gardening tools
Hand cultivators, trowels, forks,
transplanters and weeders are
among the gardening tools you'll
find at this spot.


August has all sorts of hose
couplings and nozzles, grass
shears, hedge shears and rakes.
He also has both the rotating
and tulip-type garden sprinklers.
If you're in spring gardening
mood, you'll want to investigate
Augustus stand.

Weigert's and Augustus all at

Mrs. Woodrow Wilson, widow Of
the President, was the first person
to pass through the restored door

terday.


Mrs. Wilson was among nearly
500 guests and spectators who wit

Gadsby's Tavern in June from
the Metropolitan Museum of Art
In New York City where it has
been exhibited for nearly so years.


Maj. Gen. Ulysses Grant LII,
president Of the National Council
for Historic Sites and Buildings,
recalled that it was beneath the
doorway that George Washington
stood the last time he reviewed
troops before his death.

Beef prices were higher in many
Washington area stores today, but
plentiful supplies of fresh pork
brought reductions in some pork
cuts.


Typical of the beef situation
here was one large chain which
posted an additional 2 cents a
pound on it's porterhouse and sir
loin steaks and hamburgers and 4
cents on chuck roast.


While it listed whole pork loinS
and loin chops at 2 cents above a
week ago, fresh hams, shoulder OF
pork and fresh picnics were down
2 cents a pound.


Eggs, which have been quite
scarce, were reported up one to
three cents a dozen from last
week.


Lamb and veal prices showed
little change.


Demand for Pork Increases.


Although trade sources pre-
dicted that meat prices would
start downward well before the
end of the month, there was no
indication this week that they
had reached their seasonal peak.


With cooler weather, demand
for pork was picking up. Hog
marketings were stepping up, too,
as the period of heavy slaughter
approached.


The beef market, on the other
hand, was caught in an ir1-between
period. Choice cattle from grain
feed lots was getting scarce and
more expensive as its season
neared an end, and grass range
fed cattle was not yet arriving in
volume. -

socking four in the late innings
to come from behind and beat
the Giants, 1873.


Gene Hermanski homered with
two out and the bases loaded in
the sixth inning. to enable the
Dodgers to tie the score at 8-8.

lock in the eighth with his tenth
homer Of the season. Carl Furillo
hit an inside-the-park homer in
the top OF the ninth and Reese
followed with his second Of the
game with two mates aboard to
clinch the game for the Brooks.

Dodgers and enjoyed 40 lead

third when the Giants knocked

LISBON, Portugal, July 26.-
Portugal's premier warned his
Parliament yesterday that Russia
could carry her armies in
smashing march as far as the
British Channel and the Pyrenees
any time she wanted.


In a surprise appearance before
the Assembly, which is consider
ing ratification of the Atlantic
Pact, Premier Antonio Salazar
said the treaty deserved enthusi-
astic support since it would help
avoid the menace from the East.


He praised "the initiative of the
United States and Canada in pro-
noting" the alliance, and said
Portugal had signed after making
certain Portuguese bases would
not be used In peacetime. The
premier said a weak point might
be that Spain was left out.


The National Assembly referred
the pact to its Political and For
eign Affairs Committees. which
are expected to report favorably
tomorrow.

agency Adm.

reduced by 80 per cent.

charges and asserted the persons
named by the Soviets we're not Off
cial personnel but Yugoslav dis
placed persons.

between the Communists and the
West continued nonstop.


Press reports said the Russians
had taken direct control Of traffic
inspection measures within the city
to plug loopholes in their blockade
against Western Berlin. Henceforth,
these published reports said, certain
materials may not be transported

headquarters.

9.-Six Soviet-zone border cross

and vegetables from the Western
zones OF Germany.

on the British-Soviet zone border
and at Wartha, Neustadt. Hof and

still was reported open.

known to be closed along the
border of the American zone state
of Hesse. Neustadt. Hof and Co.

Soviet crossing guards gave nc
reason for their action except

/ telephoned orders from the Sow

snag in truck traffic, the rail situ-
alton approached normalcy.

authorities announced their mill
tary passenger trains will resume
service to Berlin Monday night

l94S, when the Soviets introduced
restrictions. 1t resumed when the
Soviet blockade was lifted last

when West Berlin railway work
ers went on strike a few days
later.

VIENNA, Austria, Mar. IAN
American soldier and his Austrian
girl friend were beaten by three
men in Russian uniform in the
Soviet sector of Vienna Sunday
night, the provost marshals office
announced yesterday. Both suf-
fered face bruises.


The soldier was Pfc. Grady F
Green of South Carolina. His
companion was Frederick To-
mesh, who lives in the Russian
sector of the city.


Military police, who are investi-
eating the incident, said the couple
was stopped near the Tomesh
home about 10 pm. They said
one of the men asked Pvt. Green
in German for his Identification
papers. Both Pvt. Green and the
girl showed their papers and gave
their nationality.


AS they were speaking, another
of the soldiers struck Pvt. Green
on the head, police said. A third
soldier then grabbed Pvt. Green
and held him while the first struck
him three times in the face, they
said.


One of the men snatched Pvt.
Green's wallet, police added. The
girl trying to escape, was grabbed
and struck on the head.


The couple finally fled into a
nearby cafe. One of the attackers
followed and threw a chair at
Pvt. Green.

Daily, Western-sector inhabit-

-Pocketbooks are searched first.

Denmark's position on the North

links to the West, as proposed

not be strong enough to make her
feel secure.


Russian Reaction Feared.
Norway. Sweden and Denmark

the West in the Marshall Plan.
Until recently. however. they had
been reluctant to forge any mill
tary links for fear of Russian re-
action. All are within easy range

the Soviet and Denmark is 10

bases. Sweden borders on Finland,

racies. The resolution said an
all l-Scandinavian alliance is mot

The three worst-battered ships

the tanker John H. Marion and
the Greek freighter Mathoes.

ported herself $50 miles east of
Nantucket this morning, making

where one storm is now centered,
the Mathoes radioed she could
no longer proceed because of the
wind and seas. although she was
in no immediate danger.


Canadian authorities were send
ing help, the Coast Guard said.

Nova Scotia storm, which moved
north from the Delaware capes,
apparently was slackening. There
still were 60-mile- hour winds
in it's center about 200 miles
southeast of Nova Scotia, how
ever.

centers south of Iceland and ex-
tends 900 miles south across the
main shipping lanes to England.
1t, too, has winds up to 60 m.p.h.,
the Bureau said, and apparently
is at its peak.


Since Sunday the two gales have
disrupted shipping schedules. with
even the superliners running a
day late.

to do with perception.

ossicles which fit snugly together,
forming a continuous exoskeleton.

externally it is almost impossible to
discover where they join. Close in
spection reveals that the countless
projections and knobs which are

Swift action on Capitol Hill
pulled number of big Govern
ment agencies out of a financial
hole today.

operating funds that should have
been voted six weeks ago still
were snarled up in Congress.
September IS is the new deadline
for solving the tangle-the third
new dead1ine Congress has set
since June 80.


Quick teamwork between Chair
men Cannon and McKellar of the
House and Senate Appropriations
Committees ended a temporary
financial emergency late yester-
day for a long list of Government
agencies which have been waiting
for passage Of their regular ap-
propriations since the new fiscal
year started July l.


Stopgap Plan Approved.


Mr.. Cannon and Senator Nc
Kellar sped approval of a stop.
gap measure so about 40 Govern
ment agencies can continue meet
ing payrolls and other expenses.


Officially the Army, Navy, Air
Force, Atomic Energy Commis-
sion, Veterans Administration,
Interior Department and more
than a score of other agencies
ran out of money at midnight
Monday.


Congress is supposed to get
money bills for Government
agencies out of the way before
the fiscal year starts.


The House did it's work weeks
ago but a stubborn and slow
moving economy drive in the
Senate has begged down six ma
jor money bills there.


Twice Congress passed stopgap
measures-one to permit reduced
spending during July and then
another for The first Is days of
August. Rebellious House mem
bers blocked the third stopgap
move earlier this week.

Mr.. Cannon finally forced a IA
vorable House vote yesterday.

approval of the new stopgap
measure. then rushed it through
the Senate by voice vote late in
the day.

President Truman's signature.

terror Department appropriation,

mittee adjusts differences. Then

again approve these compromises.

50, 900, 100000 for the Veterans.

600, 900 foreign recovery bill and

Freezing cold hit the Southern
Plains today after heavy rains
which took at least three lives in

crop at harvest time.

at several points.

hart reported an early morning
low of 26 degrees. Elk City, Okla,

two days rain which delayed the
cotton harvest but helped other
crops.

in Upstate New York and hurries

low New England temperature was

ton, Me. Canton and Massena,

Virginia.

NEW YORK, Feb. 12.-Buyers
were cautious this week as the
cotton textile market reflected
breaks in commodity and security
prices.


Early in the week there was a
feeling that prices might turn
lower If cotton quotations con-
tinued to sag. But later this
sentiment was dispelled somewhat
by q more steady performance In
the futures market.
Interest in the popular 80
square print cloth was keen and
broadcloths drew q good deal OF
attention. Other sections were
quiet.


The wool goods market wit
messed the opening Of fall lines
Of woolens and worsteds. Prices
were about unchanged from spring
levels and the trade expected other
mills would follow the trend set
by the initial group.


Through the policy Of un-
changed prices mills will be abb
sorbing q good deal of the raw
wool price increases. Raw wool
is still holding at record levels in
the world market.


Rayon goods were dull. Sales
continued spotty. With produc-

ample for market needs, con-
verters were taking cloth only as
retail buyers set the pace through
purchases.

first 20 years they stick closely to
their pyramidal pattern Of growth.
Then the lower limbs become more

Once there was little girl whose
name was Sally Ann. Her mother
sent her to the store across the park
in front of her home. 1t was BEAU
tiful, sunny day, and when Sally Ann
crossed the park, she sat down on a
bench in the nice warm sun. She
began to feel sleepy.


Suddenly she saw a little monkey.
She got up to follow the little mon
key and he led her into a deep wood.
Sally Ann began to feel strange.
She saw many animals all around
her, and suddenly the animals began
to chase her. She ran deeper into
the wood, and then saw pretty
little house.


Sally Ann did not know that the
Witch of the Forest lived there. The
Witch caught her as she walked to-
ward the little house. Sally Ann was
very frightened. The Witch kept
her for many days and made her
work very hard.


One night when the Witch was
sleeping, Sally Ann climbed out of
the window. Alas, she did not watch
where she was running and she fell
into an old well.


She screamed, Help, help!" Her
screams woke the animals Of the
wood. The little monkey reached
her first. He was q smart monkey
and he pulled her out Of the well.


BY this time the Witch was awake.
She discovered that Sally Ann was
gone and she took her spy glass to
look for her. Soon she spied Sally
Ann and the little monkey.


With her magic power, the Witch
began to draw Sally Ann toward her,
but Sally Ann guessed what was
happening. She knew the Witch
could not draw trees to her, so she
caught hold of big oak tree.


There was only one thing the
Witch could do, and she started run
ming toward Sally Ann. Sally Ann
was very frightened, but being q
brave, smart girl, she got an idea.
She broke small branch OF the
tree, and she climbed up the tree.


When the old Witch arrived, Sally
Ann said to her, Come on up you
horrible old thing"


How dare you call me that, you
wretched girl" said the Witch, and
she began climbing the tree.


When the old Witch was close
enough, Sally Ann began to tickle
her with the branch that she had
broken of. The Witch sneezed, "Ah
choo, ali choo!" She sneezed so
hard she fell out of the tree and
broke her neck. If you ask me, it
was what she deserved.


Sally Ann spent the rest Of the
night in the tree, and before she
knew it, it was dawn. Some hunters
had come to the wood. One of the
hunters mistook Sally Ann for an
animal and shot at her.


Suddenly she was falling down,
down, down.


And then she woke up and found
herself lying beside the park bench.
On the street q car had stopped be-
cause tire had blown out.


All the time, Sally Ann had been
dreaming. She got up, brushed her
self OF and ran home. She was glad
to see her mother.

CABANATUAN, Philippines.
April 28.-All is far from peace

Philippines.


Readiness for trouble is evident
on all sides and already violence
flares sporadically. Today's am
bush murder of Mrs. Aurora Que
zon. her daughter and others was
only the latest incident to occur.


Other recent incidents include
the ambush murder of a police
chief, wounding of four civilians
by a grenade thrown by a drunken
soldier, death of Philippine
Scout of the United States Army
in a mass holdup, and alerting
of this provincial capital of 55.-
900 against possible attack by
marauders.


Driving over the countryside
less than 100 miles north of
Manila, one finds villagers
thronging the roads by day. At
sundown all roads are clear. The
few travellers drive at high speed.


Police Heavily Armed.


Philippines constabulary and
temporary police. all heavily
armed, stand guard in even the
smallest villages.


Families keep close to their
homes. Many have dug foxholes
beneath their stilt-legged nipa-
palm huts.


What is the reason for all this?
Why. this is "huklandia." the
stamping ground of the outlawed,
Communicated peasants called

Tagalog for Peoples Anti-Japa-
nese Army" 1t was organized

japanese, and kept going after
ward in opposition to the Philip
pines government.


The people fear the Huks, the
civilian guards and the soldiers,
and the bloody clashes that come
when one group meets the other.


Last fall and winter the con-
stabulary mounted stiff cam
paign against the Huks. The
government had attempted previ-
ously to make a deal, offering
amnesty If the Huks would sur
render their arms. Mutual dis
trust was too strong, and the
peace talks broke down.


Hideouts Attacked.


Then the soldiers and tempo

of the dissidents. More than 500

Survivors fled in small bands east
to the Sierra Madre and west to
the Xambales Mountains. Their
leader, Taruc. an avowed Com
munist, went underground.


Late in February. the govern
ment ran out of the fund it had
used to pay temporary police. The

BERLIN. June 4.-West Berlin
rail strikers offered new terms to-
day for settlement Of a two-week
walkout which has halted all train
traffic.


The strikers proposed to the
Russian sponsored rail manage
ment that the railroad divide itself
into East and West sections like
everything else in Berlin. Under
the plan the West section would
do business with the striking anti
Communist union and the East
section with the nonstriking Com
munist union.


There was no immediate indi-
cation whether the idea would be
considered favorably by the Soviet
controlled railway.


American officials said today
that despite the rail strike. West
.ern Berliners have greater supplies
of food and coal than at any time
since 1945. They said West Ber-
lin now has a 60-day reserve. Just
before the Soviets lifted their bar
riers May IL, the West was down
to a skinny three-week reserve.


Nothing Moving by Rail.


From the time of the lifting of
the blockade until the railway
strike the railways brought in $780,
900 tons of supplies. Nothing is
being moved by rail now but
trucks and barges are bringing in
1000 tons daily and the airlift
between 5000 and 1000 tons daily.


j. w. Darling. economics official
of the American Military Govern
ment's city element. said the net
result Is that West Berliners are
now getting a daily rationed diet
averaging 1000 calories and an
extra 800 calories from unrationed
foods.

demand that workers be paid in

Maryland State police today wired
warrant to Tampa, Fla, for the
arrest of one Washington youth and
sought court clearance for warrants
against two others in connection
with the 4,400 robbery of a jewelry
store near Fort Meade January 2.


The three boys, Tampa police
said, have been charged with rob-
berry of two Tampa homes. Police
said they also have admitted rob-
berries of a Boomtown store near
Fort Meade, a Boy Scout camp at
Winchester. Va. and entering a
home in Green Cove Springs, Fla.


Washington police said jewelry
believed taken from the Maryland
store was recovered last night from
couch in the Southeast Washing
ton home of one of the boys, who is
II years old. The other two, BROTH
ers, are 16 and 18 years old, police
said.


The Maryland warrant has been
wired to Tampa for arrest of the
18-year-old boy, police said, but they
must get clearance from Juvenile
Court authorities in order to issue
warrants for the other two.
